one_line_idea: The layer-wise need for adaptation in SAM is U-shaped: earliest and final encoder layers require updates while the middle two-thirds are domain-universal, contradicting both adapt-everything and adapt-last-layers defaults.
problem: PEFT parameter budgets are spread uniformly or concentrated late by convention, without a map of where domain-specific computation actually lives in a segmentation ViT.
core_hypothesis: Early layers encode sensor and texture statistics (shift-sensitive), late layers interface with the decoder's expectations (shift-sensitive), and middle layers compute generic grouping (shift-tolerant), so per-layer adaptation gain follows a U-shape across depths and across domains.
falsifiable_prediction: Single-layer LoRA insertions evaluated per depth on several domains trace a U-shaped gain curve, and a budgeted allocation matching the U-shape beats uniform and last-k allocations at equal parameters.
why_important: A validated adaptation map cuts PEFT cost, and the U-shape (if real) is evidence for a three-phase functional organization of dense-prediction transformers.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: layer-wise probing exists for classification ViTs; a per-layer adaptation-gain map for promptable segmentation with an allocation test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For SAM-B on three domains, train 12 single-layer LoRA variants plus allocation arms; falsified if gain is flat or monotone in depth.
main_risk: Single-layer gains may not compose additively, weakening the allocation corollary even if the U-shape holds.
community_default_belief: Later layers are more task-specific, so adapting them (or everything) is the sensible default.
why_it_might_be_wrong: That heuristic comes from classification, where semantics concentrate late; dense grouping may instead be generic in the middle with domain-coupling at both interfaces.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: three single-layer LoRAs (early, middle, late) on one domain; a middle-layer minimum is immediate support.

one_line_idea: SAM's windowed-attention design leaves a grid fingerprint: under domain shift, segmentation errors cluster along the window boundaries of the ViT, an architecture-induced spatial artifact nobody audits for.
problem: Error analyses treat mistake locations as image-driven; if a fixed architectural grid systematically seeds errors, then error maps are partially artifacts of engineering choices, and tiling or padding decisions interact with it invisibly.
core_hypothesis: Because most encoder layers use windowed attention with only sparse global layers, cross-window integration is weaker, and under shift (where features are noisier) mask boundary errors and mask fragmentation align with the internal window lattice at rates far above chance.
falsifiable_prediction: Averaging error maps over many shifted-domain images in encoder-grid coordinates reveals periodic structure at the window frequency, absent in-distribution or in a full-attention variant at matched accuracy.
why_important: It exposes a class of architecture-induced, spatially-structured failure invisible to scalar metrics, with direct implications for how images should be tiled and padded and for the design of efficient attention in dense models.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: window artifacts are known in image restoration models; a quantitative audit for promptable segmentation under shift appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Accumulate per-pixel error frequencies in grid coordinates over 1000 shifted images, test for periodicity via Fourier analysis of the aggregate map; falsified if no window-frequency peak exists.
main_risk: Object-position biases in datasets could masquerade as periodicity; randomized image offsets are needed as controls.
community_default_belief: Windowed attention with a few global layers is functionally equivalent to full attention for segmentation quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Equivalence was validated in-distribution where redundancy masks integration weaknesses; shift removes the redundancy and exposes the lattice.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 200 shifted images with random offsets, aggregate error map, look for lattice peaks in its spectrum.

one_line_idea: Despite being trained to find boundaries, SAM remains texture-biased in the cue-conflict sense: when shape and texture disagree, its groupings follow texture, showing that segmentation training does not confer shape bias.
problem: The community tacitly assumes a model that segments everything must understand shape; if SAM's grouping is texture-driven, its failures on camouflage, stains, and shadows are principled and predictable rather than random edge cases.
core_hypothesis: Class-agnostic mask training rewards locally-consistent-region detection, which texture statistics support more cheaply than global shape, so SAM's decisions in cue-conflict stimuli (shape of A, texture of B) side with texture at rates comparable to ImageNet-trained ViTs.
falsifiable_prediction: On segmentation-adapted cue-conflict stimuli (objects with transplanted textures, texture boundaries crossing shape boundaries), SAM's masks follow texture boundaries against shape boundaries in the majority of conflicts, and PEFT on shape-critical domains reduces this only marginally.
why_important: Shape-vs-texture bias shaped the robustness literature for classification; establishing the segmentation analogue defines which robustness interventions transfer and explains a family of SAM failures with one mechanism.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: cue-conflict methodology exists for classifiers (Geirhos et al.); a rigorous segmentation-native adaptation measuring grouping decisions under conflict appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 300 cue-conflict segmentation stimuli with unambiguous shape-defined ground truth, prompt SAM, score texture-following rate against human annotators as reference; falsified if SAM is shape-dominant.
main_risk: Synthetic stimuli may be out-of-distribution enough that behavior reflects distribution shift, not cue preference; naturalistic conflict cases (camouflage datasets) should corroborate.
community_default_belief: Training on a billion masks teaches shape; SAM's boundary acuity implies shape understanding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary acuity requires only local contrast sensitivity; nothing in the objective requires global shape representation, and shortcut theory predicts the cheaper cue wins.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 30 texture-transplant stimuli, click centers, tally whether masks stop at texture or shape boundaries.

evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK: cue-conflict texture-bias methodology (Geirhos et al. 2019) exists for classification

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept but flagged: cue-conflict paradigm port to SAM; prior-art search mandatory (texture-bias literature is crowded).

one_line_idea: Token-norm inflation under domain shift maps where adaptation is needed: per-layer feature-norm statistics on unlabeled target images predict the optimal LoRA placement, enabling data-driven adapter allocation without any labels.
problem: Adapter placement is chosen blind; a label-free diagnostic that localizes shift within the network would let practitioners spend parameters exactly where the model is struggling.
core_hypothesis: Layers whose token-norm and activation-statistics deviate most from natural-image reference statistics under target-domain inputs are the layers where LoRA insertion yields the largest gain, because statistical deviation marks broken computations.
falsifiable_prediction: Across domains, rank correlation between per-layer statistical-deviation scores (computed on unlabeled target images) and measured per-layer single-LoRA gains is strong; allocation guided by deviation beats uniform allocation at matched budgets.
why_important: It would turn PEFT configuration from folklore into measurement, and validate a general principle that internal-statistics drift localizes damage in foundation models.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: activation-statistics monitoring exists for OOD detection; using it prescriptively to allocate adaptation capacity in segmentation models appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For three domains, compute per-layer deviation profiles, then train single-layer LoRAs per depth to get ground-truth gain profiles, correlate; falsified if correlation is weak or inconsistent.
main_risk: Deviation might mark layers reacting to shift rather than layers whose repair helps, breaking the prescriptive link even if the descriptive one holds.
community_default_belief: Where to place adapters is a hyperparameter to sweep, not something the network's own statistics can tell you.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Statistical drift is the visible symptom of computation operating off-manifold, and repairing off-manifold computation is what adaptation does, so symptom location and repair location plausibly coincide.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: one domain, deviation profile vs three single-layer LoRA gains (early, middle, late); rank agreement is a quick signal.

one_line_idea: Aspect-ratio distortion from SAM's square-padded resizing is a first-order hidden failure source for thin elongated structures, rivaling texture shift in damage but fixable by inference-time letterboxing choices alone.
problem: Domain-gap discussions focus on appearance, ignoring that preprocessing geometry (fixed square input, positional-embedding interpolation) deforms structure statistics; blame is misassigned and cheap fixes are missed.
core_hypothesis: Performance loss on thin-structure domains decomposes into an appearance component and a preprocessing-geometry component, with the geometry component dominating when structures are near the internal resolution limit; changing only padding, tiling, and positional-embedding handling recovers it.
falsifiable_prediction: A factorial evaluation crossing appearance (native vs style-matched) with preprocessing (default vs geometry-preserving) on thin-structure datasets attributes a larger share of the frozen-model deficit to preprocessing than to appearance, opposite to the community's implicit attribution.
why_important: If a leading cause of failure is a controllable engineering choice, many reported domain gaps are inflated, and PEFT gains partly re-learn what better preprocessing gives for free.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: individual tricks (tiling, high-res variants) are known; a controlled attribution decomposing preprocessing geometry vs appearance shift appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two thin-structure datasets, 2x2 factorial (appearance matching x geometry-preserving preprocessing), frozen SAM; falsified if appearance dominates the decomposition everywhere.
main_risk: Geometry-preserving inference (tiles, overlaps) changes compute and context; fairness of comparison requires care.
community_default_belief: SAM fails on thin structures because such masks are rare in web-image training data (an appearance and prior problem).
why_it_might_be_wrong: A structure two internal-pixels wide is unresolvable regardless of priors; the resolution and distortion bottleneck logically precedes the prior-based explanation but is rarely isolated.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: one dataset, default vs tiled geometry-preserving inference with frozen SAM; the gap between them bounds the preprocessing component.

one_line_idea: SAM is unusually sensitive to JPEG and resampling artifacts because SA-1B consisted of high-quality licensed photography, making compression level an unmodeled domain axis that hits SAM harder than supervised baselines.
problem: Real-world pipelines feed SAM heavily compressed or re-encoded images (screenshots, telemedicine, drone links), but robustness studies emphasize weather and noise corruptions, leaving codec-induced shift unquantified.
core_hypothesis: The pretraining corpus's uniformly high image quality created a quality-blind spot: boundary-acuity features exploit high-frequency detail that compression destroys, so SAM's boundary quality degrades faster with compression strength than that of models trained on messy web data.
falsifiable_prediction: Boundary-F scores as a function of JPEG quality decline with a steeper slope for frozen SAM than for segmentation baselines trained on standard (compression-diverse) datasets, and the loss concentrates in boundary precision rather than region recall.
why_important: Compression is the single most common transformation applied to images in the wild; a documented codec fragility would change deployment guidance and motivate quality-diverse pretraining or augmentations.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: corruption benchmarks include JPEG as one entry, but a focused analysis of quality-distribution mismatch traced to the pretraining corpus, with boundary-decomposed metrics, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate frozen SAM and two baselines across a JPEG-quality ladder on shared benchmarks with boundary-decomposed metrics; falsified if SAM's slope is not steeper.
main_risk: Attribution to corpus quality (rather than architecture) needs an extra control, e.g., an augmentation-retrained variant, which adds cost.
community_default_belief: SAM's scale makes it robust to mundane perturbations like compression; robustness concerns center on weather, blur, and noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scale conveys robustness only to variation present in the data; SA-1B's curation plausibly removed exactly this variation, and boundary precision depends on the frequencies compression removes first.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 100 images at 4 quality levels, frozen SAM boundary-F curve vs one baseline.

evidence_label.prior_work_basis: KNOWN FACT: SA-1B was built from licensed high-resolution photography per the SAM paper

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: compression fragility from SA-1B quality blind spot; direction distinct from B-045's artifact-as-cue claim.

one_line_idea: SAM's encoder exhibits high-norm outlier tokens (register-like sinks), and their spatial positions correlate with mask leakage errors, linking a known ViT pathology to concrete segmentation failures for the first time.
problem: Outlier tokens are documented in classification ViTs as a global-information artifact, but whether they exist in SAM and whether they matter for dense outputs is unknown; if they seed localized errors, a known cure (register tokens) becomes an adaptation-free fix.
core_hypothesis: SAM's encoder develops a small set of high-norm tokens at semantically vacant positions; because the decoder reads the spatial feature map directly, these positions carry corrupted local information and are enriched among pixels where masks leak or fragment.
falsifiable_prediction: High-norm token locations are stable per image, and conditional error rates at those locations exceed matched-control locations significantly; adding trained register tokens (with brief adapter-level tuning) reduces exactly those errors without moving other metrics.
why_important: It would connect representation pathology research to dense-prediction quality with a causal repair, and provide a concrete mechanism for a subset of hitherto-unexplained SAM errors.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: outlier tokens and registers are established for classification ViTs (Darcet et al.); their dense-prediction consequences in SAM appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Detect high-norm tokens across 1000 images, test error enrichment at their positions with matched controls; then a register-tuning intervention arm; falsified if no enrichment or no targeted repair.
main_risk: SAM's segmentation training may have suppressed outlier formation, yielding a clean null (itself informative but less publishable).
community_default_belief: Outlier tokens are a curiosity of classification ViTs with no established consequence for dense prediction quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense decoders consume every spatial position, so a pathology harmless under global pooling becomes load-bearing; nobody has looked because the pathology was discovered in a different subfield.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: token-norm maps for 50 images, overlay with SAM error maps, visual plus statistical check of co-location.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (outlier tokens documented in ViTs, e.g., registers paper by Darcet et al. 2023)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK for the pathology in classification ViTs; SAM-specific claims are MODEL SPECULATION

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept but flagged: register-token pathology port; retained for the concrete link to mask-leakage errors.

one_line_idea: The two-layer mask decoder, not the encoder, is the binding constraint for dense thin structures: deepening only the decoder (keeping the encoder frozen) recovers vessel- and crack-like segmentation that encoder PEFT cannot, at a fraction of the parameters.
problem: Thin-structure failure is attributed to encoder resolution and priors, driving expensive encoder-side interventions, but nobody has tested whether the decoder's two rounds of cross-attention simply cannot propagate connectivity information along elongated structures.
core_hypothesis: Segmenting elongated connected structures requires iterative evidence propagation proportional to structure length; two decoder layers implement a fixed small number of propagation steps, so failures scale with structure tortuosity and are relieved by decoder depth, not encoder adaptation.
falsifiable_prediction: Error rate on thin structures increases with geodesic length-to-width ratio under frozen SAM; adding decoder layers (trained on modest data, encoder frozen) flattens this curve, while encoder LoRA at matched parameters does not.
why_important: It relocates a famous failure mode from the expensive component to the cheap one, changes adaptation strategy for a large application family, and provides an interpretable computational account (propagation depth) of a failure.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: decoder modifications for quality exist (e.g., HQ-SAM adds tokens and features), but the propagation-depth account of thin-structure failure with a tortuosity-stratified test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stratify a vessel-like dataset by tortuosity, evaluate frozen SAM, decoder-deepened SAM, and encoder-LoRA SAM at matched trainable parameters; falsified if decoder depth does not preferentially fix high-tortuosity errors.
main_risk: Deepened decoders must be trained, so gains could come from extra data exposure rather than depth; parameter- and data-matched controls are essential.
community_default_belief: Thin-structure failure stems from the encoder's internal resolution and pretraining priors; the decoder is a sufficient lightweight head.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Cross-attention with a handful of tokens over a coarse grid gives few sequential integration steps, while linear structures demand many; the encoder may already represent the structure that the decoder cannot trace.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: freeze everything, train a 4-layer decoder clone vs the standard 2-layer on the same small vessel dataset, compare tortuosity-stratified curves.

evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK: HQ-SAM (Ke et al. 2023) improves mask quality via decoder-side changes; the propagation-depth mechanism is MODEL SPECULATION

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: SAM's mask tokens are overloaded scale-generalists: forcing token specialization by object scale (a handful of scale-conditioned output tokens) tests whether token capacity, not feature quality, limits small-object segmentation.
problem: Small-object failure is blamed on features or resolution, but a single learned output token must serve objects across four orders of magnitude of area, and the token-capacity explanation has never been isolated.
core_hypothesis: A single output token's query vector cannot be simultaneously optimal for all scales, so the effective operating point is biased toward the training-mass scale; adding scale-dedicated tokens (trained briefly, all else frozen) disproportionately improves off-modal scales.
falsifiable_prediction: Scale-stratified accuracy of frozen SAM shows depressed performance at scale extremes; a token-specialized variant trained on the same data redistributes accuracy toward extremes, while an equally-parameterized non-specialized control does not.
why_important: It probes whether the query-token bottleneck is a real capacity limit in promptable architectures, informing decoder design beyond SAM (any DETR-style promptable head).
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: multi-token decoders exist for quality (HQ-SAM) and ambiguity (SAM itself), but scale-conditioned token specialization as a causal test of token overload appears untried.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 3 scale-conditioned tokens vs 3 unconditioned extra tokens (control) on identical data with frozen backbone; compare scale-stratified gains; falsified if both arms move identically.
main_risk: Scale conditioning requires knowing scale at inference; a scale-router adds complexity that may absorb the gains.
community_default_belief: Output tokens are flexible queries; failures at scale extremes come from features and internal resolution, not from token capacity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In DETR-style systems queries famously specialize by location and size on their own, suggesting one shared query serving all scales is an unnatural operating regime that training mass will bias.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours for the descriptive half: scale-stratified accuracy curve of frozen SAM on one instance dataset to confirm the off-modal depression exists and is large.

one_line_idea: SAM has a constant systematic boundary offset (not proportional jitter) traceable to its 4x upsampling path, which means a universal sub-pixel correction could improve every SAM output at zero model cost.
problem: Boundary error is treated as stochastic and content-driven; if a fixed directional or radial bias exists from the transposed-convolution upsampler, all downstream measurements (areas, volumes, morphometrics) are biased, and a post-hoc correction is free accuracy.
core_hypothesis: The learned upsampling path induces a content-independent boundary displacement field (systematic erosion or dilation of a fixed sub-pixel magnitude, possibly orientation-dependent), detectable by aggregating signed boundary errors over many objects and correctable by a fixed morphological adjustment.
falsifiable_prediction: Signed distance between predicted and true boundaries, aggregated over thousands of straight-boundary segments, has a nonzero mean of consistent sign across datasets, roughly independent of object size and texture; applying the inverse offset improves boundary-F everywhere.
why_important: A universal correction improving all deployments is rare low-hanging fruit, and the measurement methodology (signed aggregate boundary bias) would become a standard audit for any dense predictor.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: boundary quality is heavily studied, but decomposition into constant systematic bias vs proportional jitter, and attribution to the upsampling path, appears missing for SAM.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Aggregate signed boundary error over three datasets stratified by orientation and scale; falsified if mean bias is near zero or sign-inconsistent across datasets.
main_risk: Annotation conventions (annotators biased inward or outward) could produce the same signature; multi-dataset consistency and synthetic-image controls are the discriminator.
community_default_belief: Boundary errors are content-dependent noise; there is no free constant to subtract.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learned transposed convolutions are known to produce systematic phase biases in other dense tasks, and SAM's logits are thresholded at a fixed value that need not coincide with the true boundary level set.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: synthetic images with exactly known boundaries (rendered shapes), measure signed offset distribution of frozen SAM masks.

one_line_idea: Promptable segmentation cannot express relationally-defined regions (the gap between two objects, the part of A occluded by B), a representational blind spot of prompt-as-locator interfaces that no amount of PEFT fixes.
problem: The prompt interface assumes every desired region is an appearance-coherent thing a point or box can indicate, but many practically-needed regions are defined by relations between things; the boundary of this expressible set has never been mapped.
core_hypothesis: SAM's decoder implements approximate appearance-similarity expansion around the prompt, so regions whose definition requires relations rather than appearance coherence (gaps, shadows-of, occluded-parts-of) sit outside the reachable output set regardless of prompt engineering, and PEFT shifts but does not remove the boundary.
falsifiable_prediction: On a taxonomy of region types (appearance-coherent, boundary-coherent, relational), exhaustive prompt search achieves high best-IoU for the first two classes and drastically lower for relational regions, and LoRA on relational examples improves in-category performance only marginally compared to its effect on appearance categories.
why_important: Mapping the expressiveness frontier of promptable interfaces tells the field what promptability can and cannot deliver, motivating relation-aware prompt types rather than more adaptation of the same interface.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: individual failure anecdotes exist; a systematic expressiveness taxonomy with reachability measurement (best achievable IoU over exhaustive prompts) appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate 100 relational and 100 matched appearance-coherent regions, run exhaustive prompt search (points, boxes, multi-point combos) for best-IoU, then a LoRA arm on relational training data; falsified if relational best-IoU is comparable or trains up easily.
main_risk: Exhaustive prompt search is approximate; claiming unreachability requires careful search-budget arguments.
community_default_belief: With the right prompts (or light fine-tuning), SAM can segment anything a user can indicate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The decoder's computation is anchored to appearance affinity with the prompted location; relational regions have no anchoring appearance, so the failure is architectural, not a data gap.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 20 gap-between-objects cases, dense prompt search, record best achievable IoU; uniformly low values are immediate signal.

one_line_idea: The hypernetwork MLP mapping mask tokens to dynamic convolution weights in SAM is effectively linear: distilling it to a linear map costs almost nothing, revealing that the decoder's expressive component is placed where expressivity is not used.
problem: Architectural components are assumed to earn their nonlinearity; if SAM's dynamic-filter generator operates in a linear regime, the field misunderstands where the decoder's actual work happens, which matters for compression and for redesign.
core_hypothesis: Across prompts and images, the token-to-filter MLP's input-output map is well-approximated by its best linear fit (high R-squared), and swapping in the linear fit changes masks negligibly; the decoder's nonlinear work is concentrated in attention, not filter generation.
falsifiable_prediction: A linear surrogate for the hypernetwork, fit on activations from a modest image set, preserves mask outputs above 0.95 IoU on held-out images, while the same procedure applied to attention layers fails badly.
why_important: It identifies dead expressivity in a widely-copied architecture, enables cheaper decoder variants, and demonstrates a general audit (linear-regime detection) applicable to any hypernetwork component.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: linear-regime analyses exist for classifiers; auditing SAM's dynamic-filter path specifically appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit linear surrogate on 1000 prompts, evaluate output fidelity on 1000 held-out prompts across two datasets; falsified if fidelity is low in-distribution.
main_risk: Linearity may hold in-distribution but break exactly on hard or shifted cases, inverting the practical conclusion; shifted-domain fidelity must be measured too.
community_default_belief: Each decoder component, including the filter-generating MLP, contributes necessary nonlinear computation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hypernetwork-style paths often collapse to low effective rank and near-linear behavior when trained with strong upstream representations, but nobody checks after publication.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: fit and swap on 100 images, histogram output IoU between original and surrogate.

one_line_idea: Prompt tokens dilute output tokens in decoder self-attention: SAM's accuracy degradation with many clicks is an attention-budget artifact with a predictable functional form, fixable by attention masking rather than retraining.
problem: Users adding more clicks expect monotone improvement, but heavily-prompted SAM sometimes worsens; if the cause is attention dilution (output token's attention mass spread over many prompt tokens), the fix is architectural bookkeeping, not more training.
core_hypothesis: As prompt-token count grows, the output token's self-attention allocation to informative tokens shrinks roughly inversely, degrading integration; renormalizing or masking self-attention at inference restores monotonicity without weight changes.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy vs click-count curves plateau then dip for standard SAM, with dip onset predicted by measured attention-mass dilution; an inference-time attention renormalization removes the dip on the same prompts.
why_important: Monotone-improvement-with-more-input is a basic usability contract for interactive systems; diagnosing and repairing its violation via mechanism (not retraining) shows the value of mechanistic analysis for product-level fixes.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: many-click degradation is anecdotally known; the attention-dilution mechanism with a training-free intervention appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure accuracy and output-token attention mass vs click count (1 to 24) on 300 objects; then apply attention renormalization and re-measure; falsified if no dip exists, or the dip persists under renormalization.
main_risk: Degradation may instead come from conflicting click semantics (later clicks in ambiguous positions), requiring careful simulated-click protocols that keep information content fixed while varying count.
community_default_belief: More clicks give the model strictly more information, so performance should not degrade; observed dips are user error.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Softmax attention is a fixed budget; adding tokens mechanically dilutes it, and SAM's training saw mostly few-click episodes, leaving the many-click regime uncalibrated.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 30 objects, scripted informative clicks up to 20, plot the curve; a reproducible dip plus dilution measurements is the first checkpoint.

one_line_idea: Encoder-side PEFT breaks an implicit encoder-decoder contract in SAM: feature drift makes the frozen decoder's cross-attention read features it was never calibrated for, and a contract-violation metric predicts when joint (vs encoder-only) tuning is required.
problem: Recipes freeze the decoder during encoder adaptation to save parameters and preserve promptability, assuming decoder tolerance to feature change; there is no measure of when this assumption fails and silently caps adaptation gains.
core_hypothesis: The frozen decoder tolerates feature drift up to a threshold measurable as divergence of decoder cross-attention statistics (entropy, focus location) from their pretraining regime; beyond it, encoder-only tuning saturates and joint tuning pulls ahead, with the threshold consistent across domains.
falsifiable_prediction: Across adaptation runs, the gap between encoder-only and joint tuning correlates strongly with the contract-violation metric measured on the encoder-only model, enabling a decision rule that predicts (before running joint tuning) which regime a domain is in.
why_important: It converts a folklore recipe choice into a measurable criterion and characterizes modular tolerance in composite foundation models, relevant wherever frozen heads consume adapted backbones.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: freeze-vs-joint comparisons exist per-paper; an interface-drift metric that predicts the comparison outcome appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Six domains, encoder-only and joint arms, compute attention-statistic divergence on encoder-only checkpoints, correlate with the joint-minus-encoder-only gap; falsified if no predictive relationship.
main_risk: Attention statistics may drift benignly; the metric needs a null model of harmless drift to avoid false alarms.
community_default_belief: The decoder is robust to encoder adaptation; freezing it is safe and standard.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The decoder's two layers were trained against one specific feature distribution; nothing regularizes adapted features to stay readable, and two layers have little capacity to absorb distributional surprise.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: one hard domain, encoder-only vs joint runs, plus the divergence measurement; a big gap co-occurring with big divergence is the first confirmation.

one_line_idea: SAM's decoder cannot represent holes below a scale threshold: mask topology is systematically simplified (genus reduced) as hole size shrinks, defining a topological failure family with a measurable critical scale.
problem: Applications needing topologically-correct masks (rings, perforated parts, loops of vasculature) rely on SAM without knowing that its architecture may impose a resolution-dependent topology filter that silently closes holes.
core_hypothesis: The coarse internal grid plus smooth upsampling acts as a low-pass filter on the mask indicator function, so holes below a critical fraction of object scale are filled with probability approaching one, and the critical scale is predictable from the internal feature resolution and stable across content.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic annuli and perforated shapes swept across hole-size ratios, hole-preservation probability transitions sharply at a critical ratio that matches internal-resolution arithmetic, and the transition point is invariant to texture but shifts with input resolution scaling exactly as predicted.
why_important: A quantitative topology-fidelity law tells practitioners when SAM outputs can be trusted for topology-sensitive downstream tasks and gives architecture designers a concrete target (topology-preserving decoding).
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: topology-aware segmentation losses exist; a measured topological transfer function for a foundation segmenter appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthetic sweep over hole ratios, textures, and input resolutions; fit transition points; falsified if hole survival is content-dependent or does not scale with internal resolution as predicted.
main_risk: Synthetic stimuli may understate real-image performance where context cues help; a small real perforated-object set should corroborate.
community_default_belief: SAM masks are pixelwise decisions; topology errors are just boundary noise, not a systematic filter with a critical scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The mask is decoded from a 64x64-scale representation through smooth learned upsampling; representation theory says sub-grid topology cannot be encoded, but nobody has measured where the cliff sits or checked its lawfulness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: annulus sweep at one resolution, plot hole-survival vs ratio, check for a sharp transition.

one_line_idea: SAM2's memory bank induces confirmation bias: early mask errors are written to memory and then re-read as evidence, making per-object error growth superlinear after occlusions in a way promptless re-initialization would avoid.
problem: Streaming-memory tracking is celebrated for temporal consistency, but consistency is a double-edged sword: it can lock in errors; the field lacks a measurement separating error persistence caused by memory from error caused by frames being hard.
core_hypothesis: Because memory attention conditions current predictions on past predicted masks, an error written at time t raises the probability of the same error at t+1 beyond what frame difficulty explains, creating a self-reinforcing loop whose strength grows with the number of memory slots the error occupies.
falsifiable_prediction: In paired runs on identical frames where one arm has its memory surgically corrected (ground-truth mask injected at time t) and the other does not, downstream error divergence exceeds what a memoryless per-frame model shows; error autocorrelation in SAM2 exceeds frame-difficulty-matched controls and jumps after each occlusion event.
why_important: It quantifies the stability-plasticity trade-off of memory architectures with a causal method (memory surgery), guiding when trackers should distrust their own memory, and defines a general evaluation for self-conditioned video models.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: tracking drift is old knowledge, but causal attribution of drift to the memory-conditioning loop via memory-intervention experiments in SAM2 appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On videos with dense ground truth, run SAM2 with and without one-time memory correction at controlled error points, measure divergence curves; falsified if corrected and uncorrected runs reconverge quickly (memory does not perpetuate errors).
main_risk: Memory surgery requires implementation access to SAM2 internals; engineering effort could dominate.
community_default_belief: Memory improves tracking robustness; occasional drift is a price worth paying and is caused by hard frames, not by the memory mechanism itself.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Conditioning on your own outputs is a classic positive-feedback design; in language models it produces exposure-bias cascades, and SAM2's memory is architecturally analogous, yet the analogy is untested.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: 20 videos, inject a synthetic error into memory at frame k (paint a wrong mask), measure how many frames the injected error persists vs a no-injection control.

one_line_idea: SAM2's object memory encodes appearance rather than identity: repeated similar objects (twins, uniform players, identical parts) cause identity swaps at rates predictable from appearance similarity alone, exposing the absence of spatiotemporal identity binding.
problem: Users assume a video object segmenter tracks the indicated object; if memory matching is appearance-based, semantically identical distractors will capture the track, and no benchmark isolates this because standard video datasets rarely control distractor similarity.
core_hypothesis: Swap probability at crossing or proximity events is a monotone function of feature-space similarity between target and distractor, approximately independent of motion-continuity cues that would trivially disambiguate for a tracker with a motion model, revealing that memory attention lacks positional-continuity binding.
falsifiable_prediction: On a controlled benchmark of same-appearance distractor events (filmed or composited), swap rate rises steeply with appearance similarity and is barely reduced when motion continuity is made maximally informative (slow, smooth, non-overlapping paths).
why_important: It defines the identity-binding failure of memory-based video segmentation with a quantitative law, directly motivating (and providing the evaluation for) motion-aware memory designs.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: identity swaps are known in multi-object tracking; a similarity-parameterized causal characterization for promptable video segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 200 controlled distractor events by compositing (control similarity via appearance interpolation), run SAM2, regress swap rate on similarity and motion informativeness; falsified if motion cues dominate.
main_risk: Composited videos may introduce artifacts SAM2 detects; filmed twin-object sets are cleaner but harder to parameterize.
community_default_belief: SAM2 tracks the prompted object; failures happen in cluttered or fast scenes, not as lawful appearance-similarity capture in easy scenes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Memory attention retrieves by feature similarity; unless training data punished appearance-based retrieval with identical distractors (rare in web video), positional binding had no gradient pressure to emerge.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: a dozen composited crossing events at three similarity levels, count swaps; a similarity-ordered swap rate is the first signal.

one_line_idea: Video training regressed SAM2's single-image behavior in specific structure families relative to SAM1 (a capability trade nobody has mapped), so image-mode users may be silently better served by the older model.
problem: SAM2 is presented as a strict upgrade covering images and video; if temporal training reallocated capacity away from certain static-image competencies (fine boundaries, tiny objects, dense scenes), the community's default upgrade path is wrong for some users and nobody knows which.
core_hypothesis: Multi-objective training (video plus image) with shared capacity creates measurable regressions on static-image subfamilies where video supervision is misaligned with fine spatial detail, e.g., because video masks are temporally smoothed and lower-detail than SA-1B annotations.
falsifiable_prediction: A stratified image-mode audit (boundary detail, object size, scene density, structure type) shows statistically robust SAM1-over-SAM2 wins concentrated in identifiable strata, not random noise, with effect direction stable across datasets.
why_important: Model-succession decisions across the industry assume monotone improvement; a mapped regression profile would correct deployment guidance and illuminate what multi-task video training costs static perception.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: aggregate image-mode comparisons exist in the SAM2 report; a stratified regression map designed to find where the newer model loses appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run both models on several image benchmarks with stratified metrics and matched prompting, apply multiple-comparison-corrected tests per stratum; falsified if no coherent regression strata survive correction.
main_risk: Regressions may be small enough to be practically irrelevant even if statistically real; effect sizes must be reported honestly.
community_default_belief: SAM2 is at least as good as SAM1 on images, so image users should upgrade unconditionally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared-capacity multi-task training essentially always trades somewhere; the interesting question is where, and aggregate metrics are designed (unintentionally) not to show it.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: both models, one dense-scene and one fine-boundary dataset, stratified comparison with matched prompts.

one_line_idea: SAM2 has a hard forgetting horizon set by its memory capacity: reacquisition probability after occlusion collapses at a critical occlusion duration (a cliff, not a slope), and the cliff location is a fixed architectural constant rather than content-dependent.
problem: Practitioners need to know how long an object can disappear before the tracker is effectively re-initialized, but robustness is reported as averages over uncontrolled occlusion statistics, hiding whether degradation is graceful or cliff-like.
core_hypothesis: Because the memory bank holds a bounded number of recent frames plus prompted frames, occlusions longer than the effective temporal span evict all target evidence except the distant prompt, producing a sharp phase transition in reacquisition probability whose location depends on memory configuration, frame rate, and eviction policy, but only weakly on scene content.
falsifiable_prediction: Reacquisition probability vs occlusion duration (controlled synthetic occlusions on real videos) shows a sigmoid with a sharp transition; the transition point shifts predictably when memory size or frame sampling is reconfigured, and varies little across content categories.
why_important: A quantified memory horizon is an operational spec every deployment needs (how long can a surgical tool leave frame, a pedestrian be occluded), and phase-transition behavior would sharpen theory about bounded-memory streaming architectures.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: occlusion robustness is benchmarked in aggregate; a controlled duration-sweep establishing cliff-vs-slope and its architectural determinants appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Insert synthetic full occlusions of parameterized duration into 100 videos, sweep memory configurations, fit transition curves; falsified if degradation is linear or strongly content-dependent.
main_risk: Synthetic occlusion may not trigger the same occlusion-head behavior as natural occlusion; a natural-occlusion validation subset is needed.
community_default_belief: Longer occlusions are gradually harder; performance degrades smoothly with occlusion length.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Bounded-slot memories do not degrade gracefully: evidence either survives eviction or does not, which mathematically predicts a threshold effect the aggregate benchmarks average away.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 20 videos, five occlusion durations, plot reacquisition vs duration; a visible cliff answers the shape question immediately.

one_line_idea: For video domain shift, adapting only SAM2's memory-attention layers beats adapting the image encoder at equal parameter budget: domain gap in video lives in temporal association, not appearance encoding.
problem: Video PEFT recipes copy image PEFT (adapt the encoder), assuming appearance shift dominates; if association rules (how memory matches across time) are what break in new domains like medical endoscopy or thermal drones, the standard recipe misallocates all its capacity.
core_hypothesis: Cross-domain failures in video segmentation are dominated by memory retrieval errors (wrong temporal association under new motion and appearance-change statistics) rather than frame-level encoding errors, so memory-attention LoRA recovers more tracking accuracy per parameter than encoder LoRA.
falsifiable_prediction: On several shifted video domains, memory-attention-only LoRA outperforms encoder-only LoRA at matched parameters on tracking metrics while losing slightly on single-frame metrics, and the advantage grows with the domain's temporal-statistics distance from natural video.
why_important: It would establish that temporal association is a separately-adaptable competence with its own domain gap, reshaping how video foundation models are adapted and evaluated.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: PEFT for SAM2 exists in early forms; the encoder-vs-memory allocation question with temporal-statistics analysis appears open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three shifted video domains, three arms (encoder LoRA, memory LoRA, both) at matched budgets, tracking and per-frame metrics; falsified if encoder adaptation dominates everywhere.
main_risk: Public shifted-video segmentation datasets with dense annotation are scarce; may require assembling evaluation data.
community_default_belief: Adapting the image encoder is how you adapt any vision model, including video models; temporal machinery generalizes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Temporal statistics (deformation rates, illumination dynamics, camera motion) differ across domains at least as much as appearance, and memory attention was trained only on natural-video temporal statistics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: one shifted domain, two arms at small budget, compare tracking-metric recovery per parameter.

one_line_idea: SAM2's occlusion prediction is a motion-prior guess, not an evidence-based judgment: it infers disappearance from motion patterns rather than from what pixels show, failing lawfully on static occlusions and motionless disappearances.
problem: The occlusion head gates whether the model reports the object as present; if it keys on motion statistics instead of visual evidence, whole application classes (static cameras, slow scenes, objects hidden by moving occluders while stationary) inherit a systematic blind spot nobody has characterized.
core_hypothesis: Occlusion-head accuracy is high when occlusion co-occurs with characteristic motion signatures (as in web video training data) and collapses when occlusion is decoupled from motion (static object occluded by another static object after a camera pan, object occluded without either moving), revealing the head learned motion-occlusion correlation rather than visibility reasoning.
falsifiable_prediction: On a controlled battery decoupling motion from visibility (four cells: moving/static object x moving/static occluder), occlusion-head error concentrates in the decoupled cells, with error rates several times the coupled cells.
why_important: It identifies which occlusion judgments downstream systems can trust and demonstrates a shortcut-learning failure inside a headline capability of a flagship model.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: the occlusion head's decision basis appears never to have been probed with motion-visibility decoupling.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Film or composit 100 clips covering the four decoupling cells, run SAM2, compare occlusion-head confusion matrices per cell; falsified if performance is uniform.
main_risk: Constructing convincing decoupled cases at scale requires filming effort or careful compositing.
community_default_belief: The occlusion head reads visual evidence of the object being covered; its errors come from ambiguity, not from a motion shortcut.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In web video, occlusion almost always co-occurs with motion, so a motion shortcut fits training data perfectly and is cheaper to learn than visibility reasoning; shortcut theory predicts the model took it.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: ten static-occlusion clips (pan camera behind pillar while both objects static), check occlusion-head outputs against obvious ground truth.

one_line_idea: SAM2 has a preferred temporal sampling rate: tracking accuracy is non-monotone in frame rate, peaking near training-video statistics, so both slowing down and speeding up input degrades it, contrary to the assumption that more frames never hurt.
problem: Deployments choose frame rates by compute budget assuming a monotone accuracy-compute trade-off; if memory attention is tuned to a band of inter-frame change magnitudes, aggressive frame rates actively hurt, and nobody has measured the response curve.
core_hypothesis: Memory retrieval and update were optimized for the inter-frame displacement distribution of training videos, so both under-sampling (too much change per step) and over-sampling (near-duplicate frames flooding memory slots and diluting temporal diversity) reduce accuracy, producing an inverted-U response to frame rate.
falsifiable_prediction: On fixed videos re-sampled at multiple rates (with memory size held constant), tracking accuracy follows an inverted-U with an interior optimum, and the optimum shifts when memory eviction policy is modified, implicating slot competition rather than image content.
why_important: A tuned-band temporal sensitivity would change deployment guidance (higher FPS can be worse for free) and reveal that streaming memory models have a temporal operating range analogous to a resonance, a design consideration for all future streaming architectures.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: frame-rate ablations exist for trackers, but the inverted-U prediction tied to memory-slot competition, with eviction-policy manipulation as the causal test, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Resample 50 videos at five rates, run SAM2 with fixed memory config, plot accuracy vs rate; then vary eviction policy to test optimum shift; falsified if accuracy is monotone in rate.
main_risk: Ground-truth interpolation across resampled rates introduces evaluation noise; annotation-preserving resampling protocols are needed.
community_default_belief: More temporal samples give the tracker more information; high frame rate is always at least neutral for accuracy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Bounded memory means frames compete for slots; near-duplicates crowd out temporally diverse evidence, a mechanism absent from unbounded-memory intuitions the community carries over.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: five videos at three rates (quarter, native, four-x via interpolation), check for non-monotonicity.

one_line_idea: Propagation in SAM2 is temporally asymmetric beyond content effects: propagating a middle-frame prompt backward is systematically worse than forward, revealing an architectural arrow of time that batch (offline) video adaptation should exploit or repair.
problem: Offline users (annotators, editors) prompt at whichever frame is easiest and propagate both directions, assuming symmetry; a directional handicap would bias annotation quality within every produced dataset in an unexamined way.
core_hypothesis: Training predominantly on forward-streaming episodes taught memory attention forward-conditional statistics (how objects evolve forward in time), so backward propagation runs the model off its learned conditional distribution even on time-symmetric content, producing an accuracy gap that persists on reversibility-controlled clips.
falsifiable_prediction: On clips filtered for approximate time-reversal symmetry of content (no gravity-driven or causal-direction cues), forward propagation from a middle prompt outperforms backward propagation with a consistent margin, and the margin persists when clips are physically reversed (controlling content direction).
why_important: Datasets annotated with SAM2 assistance inherit direction-dependent quality gradients (later frames better than earlier), a bias that will propagate into every model trained on them; also a clean case study of temporal inductive bias in streaming architectures.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: forward-backward asymmetry with content-direction controls (reversed-clip protocol) appears unmeasured for SAM2.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select or film 100 near-time-symmetric clips, propagate from middle prompts both directions on original and reversed versions, compare accuracy in a 2x2 design; falsified if the architectural asymmetry vanishes under reversal control.
main_risk: Truly time-symmetric content is rare; the filter may leave few clips or subtle asymmetries.
community_default_belief: Propagation quality depends on content difficulty, not direction; backward equals forward for symmetric content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The model's conditional distribution was fit on one temporal direction; even on symmetric content, learned drift priors (e.g., growth vs shrinkage of masks) need not be symmetric.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 20 clips, middle prompt, both directions, paired comparison; the reversed-clip control can follow if a gap appears.

one_line_idea: Adapting SAM2 on domain video corrupts its image-mode promptability faster than adapting SAM1 on matched images does, because gradients through memory attention couple the static pathway to temporal objectives, making video PEFT uniquely forgetting-prone.
problem: Teams adopt SAM2 as their single model for images and video, then adapt it on video data; if temporal adaptation damages the image pathway disproportionately, the consolidation strategy carries a hidden tax nobody has priced.
core_hypothesis: In SAM2, image-mode behavior shares parameters with temporally-conditioned computation, so video-domain gradients perturb static-mode functions in ways image-domain gradients (in SAM1 adaptation) do not, yielding faster degradation of image-mode metrics per unit of target-domain gain.
falsifiable_prediction: Matching target-domain improvement between (a) SAM2 video-adapted and (b) SAM1 image-adapted on frames of the same domain, arm (a) shows larger drops on a fixed image-mode retention battery (natural-image click IoU, multimask diversity), consistently across domains and budgets.
why_important: It quantifies the cost of unified image-video models under adaptation, informing whether organizations should maintain separate adapted models per modality, and probes how multi-task architectures distribute adaptation damage.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: forgetting under video fine-tuning, normalized per unit target gain and compared across architecture generations, appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two domains with paired video and frame datasets; adapt SAM2 on video, SAM1 on frames, to matched target gains; run image-mode retention battery; falsified if retention losses are comparable.
main_risk: Matching target gains across different architectures and tasks is methodologically delicate; multiple matching criteria should be reported.
community_default_belief: PEFT is gentle enough that adapting the unified model on video leaves image mode essentially intact.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Temporal objectives reward temporal smoothing of features; smoothed features are exactly what fine image-mode boundary detail does not want, creating directed interference rather than random drift.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: video-adapt SAM2 on one domain briefly, run the image-mode retention battery before and after, compare to a SAM1 control.

one_line_idea: Model-in-the-loop data generation gave SAM a mask-style monoculture: SA-1B's semi-automatic pipeline filtered out messy, low-compactness masks, so SAM inherits a compactness prior that is a data-flywheel artifact, not a property of the visual world.
problem: SAM's systematic preference for smooth closed regions is treated as a neutral architectural bias, but if it was manufactured by the data engine's own filtering (stability thresholds, model-assisted annotation), then every model trained on SAM outputs compounds the artifact, and the community cannot see it because the benchmark masks share the same lineage.
core_hypothesis: The distribution of mask complexity (boundary fractal dimension, concavity counts) in SA-1B is significantly narrower than in fully-manual datasets of comparable content, and SAM's error rate grows with a target mask's distance from the SA-1B complexity mode faster than content difficulty explains.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing complexity distributions of SA-1B against manual datasets shows compression around a compact-mask mode; SAM performance stratified by target complexity shows a decline aligned with SA-1B density rather than with human difficulty ratings of the same instances.
why_important: It would document a concrete case of dataset-flywheel bias in a flagship foundation model, with a measurable signature and a clear warning for all model-assisted annotation pipelines now proliferating.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: model-in-the-loop bias is discussed abstractly; a quantitative complexity-distribution audit of SA-1B linked to SAM's error profile appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute complexity statistics for large samples of SA-1B and manual datasets; stratify SAM errors by complexity controlling for human-rated difficulty on a 500-instance subset; falsified if distributions match or errors track difficulty, not complexity-density.
main_risk: Content differences between datasets confound complexity comparisons; matched-content subsets are needed.
community_default_belief: SA-1B's scale and diversity make it a faithful sample of segmentable structure in natural images.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Its pipeline retained masks the model-in-the-loop was confident about and stable on, which mathematically skews the retained distribution toward what early models found easy: compact, smooth regions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: complexity histograms of 100k SA-1B masks vs a manual dataset; visible mode compression is the first checkpoint.

one_line_idea: SAM carries a photographic-composition prior: mask quality for identical content varies with its position in the frame (center and rule-of-thirds hotspots), an artifact of professional photography in SA-1B that surveillance and industrial imagery violates wholesale.
problem: Spatial performance heterogeneity within the frame is invisible to standard metrics, yet fixed-camera applications (inspection, retail, security) place objects anywhere, so a composition prior would translate directly into location-dependent reliability that nobody specifies.
core_hypothesis: Because professional photos concentrate subjects at compositional hotspots, SAM's per-location accuracy map (same object pasted at controlled positions) is non-uniform with peaks at center and thirds intersections, and the non-uniformity shrinks in models trained on uncurated data.
falsifiable_prediction: Paste-controlled experiments show accuracy varying by position with a pattern matching photographic composition statistics, and the pattern persists across object categories and scales, while a supervised baseline trained on uniform-position data shows a flatter map.
why_important: Position-dependent reliability is a deployment hazard with a simple audit and mitigation (position augmentation in PEFT), and the finding would add spatial composition to the catalogue of dataset biases foundation models absorb.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: center bias is known for saliency models; a quantitative positional accuracy map for promptable segmentation traced to photographic composition appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Composite 50 objects at a 5x5 position grid over diverse backgrounds, prompt identically, build the positional accuracy map; falsified if flat within noise.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts may interact with position; real translated-crop protocols should corroborate.
community_default_belief: SAM segments an object equally well wherever it appears in the frame; translation invariance is approximately assumed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: ViTs have absolute positional embeddings and the training data had strongly non-uniform object-position statistics; nothing enforces translation invariance, and the two factors compound.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: one object, 25 positions, three backgrounds; a visible center-vs-corner gap is the first signal.

one_line_idea: Class-agnostic training left latent semantics in SAM: its masks snap to semantic category boundaries even when low-level evidence contradicts them, so SAM is a covert semantic segmenter whose hidden classes bias supposedly geometry-only outputs.
problem: SAM is used as a neutral geometric tool (e.g., in scientific imaging) on the premise that it has no category preferences; if hidden semantic attractors shape its boundaries, unbiasedness claims in downstream measurement pipelines are wrong in unquantified ways.
core_hypothesis: Mask boundaries preferentially align with human category boundaries (person vs background, object vs shadow) even under adversarially-matched low-level contrast, because annotators segmented nameable things, injecting semantics into supposedly class-agnostic supervision.
falsifiable_prediction: On stimuli where a low-level boundary (contrast edge) and a semantic boundary (category edge with matched local contrast) compete, SAM sides with the semantic boundary far above chance, and the effect strength correlates with category nameability ratings.
why_important: It changes what SAM outputs mean for measurement applications and quantifies how much semantics leaks through class-agnostic annotation, a question relevant to every dataset built by asking humans to segment things.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: SAM's semantic awareness is informally noted; a controlled contrast-matched competition protocol quantifying covert semantics appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct 200 competition stimuli with photometrically matched competing boundaries, run SAM, measure semantic-side rate; falsified if near chance.
main_risk: Perfect photometric matching is hard; matching must be verified with low-level baseline models siding at chance.
community_default_belief: SAM is class-agnostic; its groupings follow visual evidence, not object categories.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The training masks were drawn around nameable objects by humans; category structure is statistically embedded in the supervision even if labels were discarded.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 20 shadow-vs-object cases where the shadow edge has stronger contrast than the object edge; count which boundary SAM follows.

one_line_idea: SAM has a viewpoint prior from licensed photography: performance drops lawfully with deviation from eye-level, subject-facing viewpoints, making overhead, egocentric, and oblique-angle imagery systematically underserved for reasons unrelated to content.
problem: Drone, robot, bodycam, and ceiling-camera imagery are huge application areas; if their deficit is a viewpoint prior rather than content difficulty, then viewpoint-targeted augmentation or adaptation would be far cheaper than the domain-specific retraining currently prescribed.
core_hypothesis: For matched scenes and objects, accuracy is a decreasing function of viewpoint distance from the photographic canon (elevation and tilt statistics of professional photos), and viewpoint explains a large share of the deficit currently attributed to domain gap in aerial and egocentric benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-view captures of the same scenes (or synthetic renders sweeping camera elevation), frozen SAM accuracy declines monotonically with elevation deviation from eye level at matched object visibility, and reweighting evaluation of an aerial benchmark by viewpoint distance accounts for most of its measured domain gap.
why_important: Correct causal attribution of the aerial and egocentric gap changes the fix (cheap viewpoint augmentation vs expensive domain pipelines) and adds viewpoint to the list of auditable foundation-model priors.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: domain gaps for aerial imagery are documented; decomposing them into viewpoint prior vs appearance content with same-scene multi-view controls appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render or capture same-scene viewpoint sweeps, measure accuracy vs elevation at controlled visibility; falsified if the curve is flat and gaps only appear with content change.
main_risk: Visibility and occlusion patterns covary with viewpoint; controls must equalize the visible-region difficulty.
community_default_belief: Aerial and egocentric imagery are hard for SAM because their content (small objects, unusual textures) differs from web photos.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Content and viewpoint were never separated: SA-1B viewpoint statistics are extremely narrow, and priors over rare conditioning variables degrade even when local appearance is familiar.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: one synthetic scene, seven camera elevations, identical objects; plot the accuracy-vs-elevation curve.

one_line_idea: SAM's part-vs-whole ambiguity resolution is anchored to SA-1B's mask-size distribution: when object-to-image size ratios leave the training regime, granularity choices become systematically biased (macro shots yield parts, distant shots yield groups) independent of prompt intent.
problem: Users at unusual magnifications (microscopy, macro photography, satellite) report SAM returning the wrong granularity; without knowing this is a lawful size-prior effect, they blame prompts or domain and reach for heavy adaptation.
core_hypothesis: The learned prior over selected-mask scale is anchored to the absolute mask-area distribution of SA-1B, so for images whose true-object area ratio is off-distribution, the top-ranked granularity shifts toward the prior mode, producing predictable part-selection at high magnification and group-selection at low magnification.
falsifiable_prediction: Zoom sweeps of the same physical object show top-ranked mask granularity switching at area-ratio thresholds aligned with SA-1B mask-size distribution quantiles, and the switch points move consistently when re-ranking by a size-prior-corrected score.
why_important: A quantitative size-prior law enables a zero-training fix (prior-corrected re-ranking) and explains a widespread cross-domain annoyance mechanistically.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: granularity instability is anecdotal; tying switch points to training-distribution quantiles and correcting by re-ranking appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Zoom-sweep protocol on 50 objects, log top-ranked mask area ratios, compare switch points to SA-1B quantiles, test the corrected re-ranker; falsified if switches are content-driven and uncorrectable by prior adjustment.
main_risk: SA-1B statistics are known, but establishing prompt-intent ground truth for granularity requires careful task design.
community_default_belief: Granularity selection reflects image ambiguity and prompt placement; magnification per se is not a systematic factor.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ranking heads regress toward training-frequency priors when the likelihood is flat; off-distribution magnifications flatten the likelihood exactly where the prior then dominates.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 10 objects, five zoom levels each, tally granularity of top-ranked masks vs zoom.

one_line_idea: Guideline archaeology: SAM's handling of pathological cases (wires, fences, reflections, transparent objects) encodes recoverable traces of SA-1B annotation-guideline decisions, showing that foundation models memorize policy, not just imagery.
problem: When SAM behaves oddly on hard structure classes, users cannot tell whether behavior reflects visual evidence or a frozen annotation-policy choice (e.g., whether annotators included holes in fences); the distinction determines whether adaptation or post-processing is the right fix.
core_hypothesis: For structure classes where annotation guidelines forced a convention, SAM's outputs are more consistent (lower cross-image entropy of topological choices) than for classes where guidelines were silent, revealing policy memorization distinguishable from evidence-driven behavior.
falsifiable_prediction: Behavioral consistency scores across structure classes are bimodal: convention-governed classes (fence holes, wire inclusion) show high consistency even across contradictory visual evidence, while guideline-silent classes show evidence-dependent variability; the partition predicts which behaviors PEFT can easily flip (policies flip fast, evidence integration does not).
why_important: Separating policy memory from perceptual competence in foundation models is a general interpretability question, and the flip-rate prediction has direct adaptation-cost implications.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: dataset-bias analyses exist, but reading annotation policy back out of a model's behavioral consistency, with a differential-adaptability prediction, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define 10 structure classes, collect 100 cases each, measure behavioral consistency and evidence-sensitivity, then fine-tune small adapters to flip each behavior and compare flip costs; falsified if consistency is uniform or flip costs do not track the partition.
main_risk: Without access to the actual guidelines, the policy-vs-evidence partition must be inferred, weakening claims; partial guideline information from the SAM paper mitigates this only partly.
community_default_belief: SAM's outputs reflect learned visual structure; annotation-protocol details wash out at a billion-mask scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Policies apply systematically across millions of masks (unlike noise, which averages out), so scale amplifies rather than washes out conventions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: fences and wires, 30 cases each, check whether hole-handling is rigidly consistent regardless of hole visibility.

one_line_idea: SA-1B's grid-prompt generation left a periodic spatial fingerprint in SAM: averaged over many images, mask-probability and mask-seed statistics show energy at the generation grid frequency, an unnoticed artifact coupling dataset construction to model prior.
problem: If the model's spatial prior carries the data engine's prompt-grid periodicity, then object detection and counting pipelines built on everything-mode inherit spatially periodic sensitivity, and dataset-construction parameters leak into every downstream model in a way nobody audits.
core_hypothesis: Masks in SA-1B's automatic stage were seeded from regular point grids, biasing the retained-mask spatial statistics; SAM internalized this as a weak periodic prior detectable by averaging click-response maps or everything-mode seed statistics over thousands of images in grid-aligned coordinates.
falsifiable_prediction: The spatial spectrum of aggregate mask-initiation statistics shows peaks at the generation-grid frequency significantly above surrogate controls (phase-randomized aggregates), and the peaks weaken in models fine-tuned on manually-annotated data.
why_important: Even a weak result establishes that dataset-generation hyperparameters imprint on foundation-model priors, motivating fingerprint audits of data engines now used everywhere (auto-labeling, model-in-the-loop pipelines).
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: periodic artifacts are studied for generative upsamplers; a data-engine fingerprint analysis for a segmentation foundation model appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Aggregate mask statistics over 10k images in normalized coordinates, spectral analysis against surrogate nulls; falsified if no grid-frequency structure exists.
main_risk: The effect, if present, is likely tiny and demands rigorous null models to avoid false positives; a null result has modest value.
community_default_belief: Dataset-construction machinery leaves no systematic trace in the trained model beyond content statistics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The grid was applied identically to millions of images; identical systematic procedures are exactly what models can and do internalize, as positional biases in other models show.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: aggregate everything-mode seed positions over 2k images, Fourier transform of the density map, look for lattice peaks.

one_line_idea: Benchmark mIoU anti-correlates with interactive usability across PEFT methods: adapters that win static benchmarks require more correction clicks in deployment because they trade prompt responsiveness for prompt-independent priors.
problem: PEFT methods for SAM are ranked by single-shot mIoU with simulated prompts, but real usage is interactive; if the ranking inverts under clicks-to-quality metrics, the community is systematically selecting the wrong methods for deployment.
core_hypothesis: Adaptation that maximizes single-shot accuracy does so partly by strengthening domain priors that override prompt details; such prior-heavy models respond weakly to corrective clicks, so single-shot accuracy and interactive efficiency are anti-correlated across adapted checkpoints within a domain.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 10+ adapted checkpoints per domain (varying method and budget), the correlation between single-shot mIoU and clicks-to-90-percent-IoU is positive (worse) rather than negative, and prompt-ablation sensitivity mediates the relationship statistically.
why_important: It would overturn the field's selection criterion for adaptation methods and introduce prompt responsiveness as a first-class evaluation axis for promptable models.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: interactive metrics exist in interactive-segmentation literature, but the claim that PEFT optimization inverts rankings between static and interactive axes, with a mediation analysis, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a grid of adapters on two domains, evaluate single-shot and simulated-interactive metrics plus prompt-ablation sensitivity, compute correlations and mediation; falsified if rankings agree across axes.
main_risk: Simulated clickers may not represent human correction behavior; a small human study would strengthen but also complicate the result.
community_default_belief: Higher benchmark mIoU means a better adapted model, full stop; interactive quality follows from static quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Single-shot metrics reward models for ignoring prompt noise, which is behaviorally identical to ignoring prompts; the metric cannot distinguish confident competence from prompt deafness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: two checkpoints with equal mIoU but different training (LoRA vs decoder-tune), compare clicks-to-quality curves; divergence at equal mIoU is the proof of concept.
