one_line_idea: Boundary metrics conflate constant offset with jitter: decomposing boundary error into bias and variance components changes which PEFT method wins, because methods differ in which component they fix.
problem: Boundary-F and HD95 summarize boundary error as a scalar, but a fixed 2-pixel dilation (correctable post hoc) and 2-pixel random jitter (a real quality problem) score identically, so method comparisons reward the wrong improvements.
core_hypothesis: PEFT methods partition into offset-fixers (whose gains vanish after optimal per-method morphological correction) and jitter-fixers (whose gains survive), and published rankings mix the two, so re-ranking after bias correction reorders a substantial fraction of comparisons.
falsifiable_prediction: Recomputing published-style comparisons with bias-corrected boundary metrics (subtract fitted constant offset before scoring) flips the winner in a meaningful fraction of method pairs, and the flip pattern is consistent across datasets.
why_important: A metric decomposition that reorders leaderboards forces cleaner claims about what adaptation methods actually improve and gives practitioners a free post-processing win where offset dominates.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: bias-variance decompositions are standard elsewhere; applying them to segmentation boundary metrics to audit PEFT comparisons appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take five adapted checkpoints across methods on two datasets, fit per-model constant offsets, recompute metrics, count ranking flips; falsified if rankings are invariant.
main_risk: Optimal offset fitting must avoid overfitting to test data; proper train-test protocol for the correction is needed.
community_default_belief: Boundary metrics measure boundary quality; a better score means better boundaries in every sense that matters.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Metrics integrate over error structure; two structurally different errors with equal integrals have very different practical costs and remediation, a distinction the community's tooling never surfaces.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: one checkpoint pair, offset-corrected re-scoring; one flip suffices to demonstrate the phenomenon exists.

one_line_idea: Centroid-click evaluation is a lucky-prompt protocol: model rankings among adapted SAMs invert under prompt distributions sampled from real user behavior, because centroid clicks are systematically easier than human clicks.
problem: Nearly all point-prompt evaluations click the object centroid or a maximally-interior point; humans click salient parts, high-contrast spots, or wherever the cursor lands first, so reported comparisons may not predict deployed rankings at all.
core_hypothesis: Model robustness to prompt-placement variation differs across adaptation methods (some narrow the prompt basin, idea 005), so the ranking of methods under centroid protocol and under human-sampled prompt distributions diverges measurably, with prompt-basin width as the mediating variable.
falsifiable_prediction: Collecting a modest set of real human click distributions (or using logged clicks from annotation tools) and re-evaluating a grid of adapted checkpoints flips method rankings in a meaningful fraction of comparisons relative to centroid protocol, and flip magnitude correlates with basin-width differences.
why_important: Evaluation realism determines which research directions look promising; documenting ranking instability under realistic prompts would redirect method development toward robustness of the prompt map rather than peak performance at an idealized prompt.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: click-simulation policies are known to matter for training; their distorting effect on evaluation rankings of adapted models appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Gather human click data on 300 objects (small user study or public annotation logs), evaluate six checkpoints under both prompt distributions, compare rankings; falsified if rankings are stable.
main_risk: Human click collection introduces its own biases (task instructions matter); multiple instruction conditions strengthen validity.
community_default_belief: Centroid or max-interior clicks are a fair, neutral standard for comparing point-prompt segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Centroid clicks maximize distance from boundary ambiguity, sampling only the easiest point of each object's prompt space; a protocol that samples one extreme cannot certify orderings over the whole space.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 30 objects with 5 self-collected human clicks each, evaluate two checkpoints under both protocols; a ranking flip at small scale motivates the full study.

one_line_idea: SAM's failures are bimodal (near-perfect or catastrophic), so mean metrics track the mixture weight rather than segmentation quality, and PEFT methods should be compared by failure-rate curves instead of averages.
problem: Two adapted models with equal mean IoU can be operationally opposite (one uniformly mediocre, one mostly perfect with rare disasters); safety-critical users need the distinction, but the literature reports means almost exclusively.
core_hypothesis: Per-instance IoU distributions for frozen and adapted SAM are strongly bimodal across domains, adaptation methods differ primarily in how they move mass between modes (not in shifting the good mode), and mean-based rankings therefore disagree with risk-based rankings (e.g., probability of IoU below 0.5) in a predictable fraction of comparisons.
falsifiable_prediction: Bimodality coefficients of per-instance IoU distributions are high across settings, method rankings under mean-IoU vs failure-rate metrics disagree substantially, and the good-mode location is nearly invariant across methods while mixture weights vary.
why_important: It changes what adaptation research optimizes (mode transport, not average lift) and equips deployment decisions with the risk-relevant statistic means cannot supply.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: per-instance variability is occasionally shown; the mixture-model account of adaptation effects and the ranking-disagreement quantification appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect per-instance IoU for a method grid on three domains, fit two-component mixtures, test mode invariance and ranking disagreement; falsified if distributions are unimodal or rankings agree.
main_risk: Bimodality may itself be an artifact of dataset heterogeneity (easy and hard subpopulations), requiring stratified analysis to locate its source.
community_default_belief: Mean IoU differences reflect quality differences; distributional details are second-order refinements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Promptable segmentation succeeds or fails at the object level (found it or grabbed the wrong thing); such all-or-nothing mechanics generate mixtures, and means over mixtures are known to mislead.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: histogram per-instance IoU for frozen SAM on one shifted dataset; visible bimodality is the entry ticket for the full study.

one_line_idea: Cross-paper PEFT-for-SAM comparisons are confounded by prompt-simulation policy more than by method: a controlled re-implementation shows the prompt protocol explains more ranking variance than the adaptation technique being advertised.
problem: Every adaptation paper picks its own prompt simulation (box jitter levels, click counts, click placement rules), making the literature an uncontrolled meta-experiment where methods and protocols vary together; the field may be accumulating conclusions about protocols while believing they are about methods.
core_hypothesis: Re-running representative PEFT methods under a crossed design (methods x prompt protocols) shows protocol main effects and method-protocol interactions comparable to or exceeding method main effects for common metric differences reported between consecutive papers.
falsifiable_prediction: Variance decomposition over the crossed grid attributes a share of ranking variance to protocol at least as large as to method, and at least one widely-cited ordering between two methods reverses under a different (equally defensible) protocol.
why_important: A demonstrated protocol confound would justify a community-standard prompt-simulation specification, improving the signal value of all future comparisons.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: protocol sensitivity is suspected informally; a quantitative variance decomposition across methods and protocols for SAM adaptation appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement four methods and four protocols on two domains with fixed seeds, run the full cross, decompose variance; falsified if method effects dominate cleanly.
main_risk: Faithful re-implementation of published methods is laborious and disputable; using released checkpoints where available mitigates.
community_default_belief: Published comparisons transfer: if method A beat method B in its paper, A is the better technique for that domain.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Prompt simulation determines task difficulty and the information the model receives; small protocol choices plausibly dwarf few-point method margins, but nobody has measured the ratio.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: two methods, two protocols, one domain; an observed interaction larger than the method margin already makes the point.

one_line_idea: Corruption robustness of SAM is prompt-type dependent in a structured way (boxes resist blur, points resist occlusion, and vice versa fails), so prompt choice is a free robustness lever no pipeline currently exploits.
problem: Robustness studies evaluate one prompt type or average over them, missing the interaction; if different prompts fail under different corruptions, deployed systems could switch prompt strategies by condition monitoring at zero model cost.
core_hypothesis: Prompt types inject different information (boxes give scale and extent priors robust to high-frequency loss; points rely on local features robust to geometric occlusion but fragile to blur), producing a structured corruption-by-prompt interaction matrix that is stable across datasets.
falsifiable_prediction: A full corruption-battery-by-prompt-type evaluation yields a significant, reproducible interaction (not just main effects), and a condition-aware prompt-selection policy derived from the matrix beats any fixed prompt type on mixed-corruption streams.
why_important: A validated interaction matrix converts robustness knowledge into an actionable inference-time policy and clarifies mechanistically what each prompt type contributes to the decoder's evidence integration.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: corruption benchmarks for SAM exist; the prompt-type interaction structure and the derived switching policy appear unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fifteen corruptions x three prompt types x two datasets with matched instances, test interaction significance and policy gains; falsified if effects are additive.
main_risk: Interaction may exist but be too weak for a policy to beat the best fixed prompt type.
community_default_belief: Robustness is a property of the model; prompts affect accuracy but corruption sensitivity is prompt-independent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Prompts determine which image evidence the decoder weights; corruptions destroy specific evidence types; the intersection is mechanically prompt-dependent, yet evaluations average over precisely this structure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: blur and occlusion x points and boxes on 100 instances; a crossed pattern in the 2x2 is the proof of concept.

one_line_idea: PEFT concentrates adversarial vulnerability: LoRA-adapted SAM is easier to attack than either frozen SAM or fully fine-tuned SAM, because low-rank updates create a small, findable subspace whose manipulation controls the whole adapted behavior.
problem: Security evaluations certify base models, and practitioners assume small parameter deltas mean small behavioral attack-surface changes; if adaptation concentrates sensitivity into a low-dimensional subspace, every adapted deployment is quietly weaker than its certified base.
core_hypothesis: Adversarial examples against LoRA-adapted models succeed at lower perturbation budgets than against frozen or fully-tuned models at matched clean accuracy, and attack gradients align measurably with the LoRA subspace, establishing concentration (not just shift) of vulnerability.
falsifiable_prediction: Attack success at fixed epsilon is ordered LoRA-adapted above fully-tuned above frozen at matched clean accuracy on the target domain, and projecting attack perturbation gradients onto the LoRA update subspace shows disproportionate alignment relative to random subspaces of equal dimension.
why_important: It connects the geometry of adaptation to security, implying rank and placement choices are security parameters, and would motivate adversarial-aware PEFT regularizers.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: robustness of fine-tuned vs frozen models is studied for classification; subspace-concentration analysis of vulnerability for segmentation PEFT appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three matched checkpoints (frozen, LoRA, full FT) on one domain, standardized attacks at several budgets plus gradient-subspace alignment analysis; falsified if orderings reverse or alignment is absent.
main_risk: Matching clean accuracy across the three regimes is nontrivial and drives the comparison's fairness.
community_default_belief: PEFT's small parameter change implies approximately the base model's robustness profile.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-rank adaptation creates a few high-leverage directions trained on little data without adversarial pressure; attackers optimize exactly for high-leverage directions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: PGD at two budgets against frozen vs one public LoRA-adapted checkpoint on the adapted domain; a large success-rate gap is the first evidence.

one_line_idea: SAM's low-contrast failures are threshold failures, not perception failures: under fog or dim light the logit landscape preserves the object (rank order intact) but the fixed binarization threshold misplaces the boundary, so an input-conditional threshold fixes fog for free.
problem: Degraded-visibility performance drives expensive enhancement preprocessing and domain adaptation, all premised on features failing; if the failure is in the final thresholding step, the community is repairing the wrong stage of the pipeline.
core_hypothesis: Global contrast reduction compresses mask logits toward the threshold without destroying their spatial ordering, so oracle-threshold masks (choosing the best cutoff per image) recover most of the clean-condition accuracy, and a lightweight contrast-conditioned threshold predictor captures most of the oracle gain.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic and real low-contrast sets, the gap between fixed-threshold and oracle-threshold performance accounts for the majority of the degradation, whereas under structural corruptions (occlusion, noise) the oracle threshold recovers little, confirming specificity.
why_important: A one-parameter inference-time fix for a whole corruption family would be immediately deployable, and the logit-preservation finding would sharpen understanding of where robustness actually breaks in dense predictors.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: adaptive thresholding is an old image-processing idea; demonstrating that a foundation segmenter's weather fragility is largely a thresholding artifact appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Contrast-degradation ladder on two datasets, compare fixed vs oracle vs predicted thresholds, plus structural-corruption controls; falsified if oracle thresholding recovers little under low contrast.
main_risk: Real fog involves scattering structure beyond global contrast; synthetic-to-real gap in the corruption model could limit the fix.
community_default_belief: Weather robustness requires robust features via augmentation, enhancement front-ends, or adaptation; the output stage is not the problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The binarization constant was calibrated on clean-image logit statistics; global input compression predictably shifts logit scale, a trivial mechanism hiding inside an impressive-looking failure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 50 images, four synthetic contrast levels, fixed vs per-image best threshold; the recovered fraction answers the core question immediately.

one_line_idea: Geometry-only prompting makes SAM structurally immune to typographic and semantic-patch attacks that fool text-conditioned segmenters, a security advantage of coordinate interfaces that quantifies the robustness cost of language conditioning.
problem: The field is racing to add text conditioning to segmentation (open-vocabulary models), implicitly assuming language grounding is a free capability upgrade; its adversarial cost relative to coordinate prompting has never been isolated with matched-architecture comparisons.
core_hypothesis: Attacks that exploit the language-vision binding (printed words, semantically suggestive patches) transfer to text-conditioned segmenters but not to coordinate-prompted SAM on the same images, and the robustness gap persists after both models are adapted to the same domain, establishing an interface-inherent (not training-data) effect.
falsifiable_prediction: On a battery of typographic and semantic-patch manipulations, text-conditioned segmentation degrades severely while point- and box-prompted SAM on identical targets degrades marginally, and hybrid models (text plus geometry) degrade in proportion to their measured reliance on the text pathway.
why_important: It provides a quantified security argument in the interface-design debate for promptable vision, relevant to safety-critical procurement decisions between text-driven and geometry-driven tools.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: typographic attacks on CLIP are established (Goh et al. documented typographic attacks on CLIP-like models); a controlled interface-level comparison for segmentation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 200 typographic and patch-attack scenes with clear target ground truth, evaluate a text-conditioned segmenter and SAM with matched prompting effort; falsified if SAM degrades comparably.
main_risk: Matched-effort prompting across interfaces is hard to define fairly; multiple prompting budgets should be reported.
community_default_belief: Text conditioning adds capability without a distinct robustness cost; attacks are a model-quality issue, not an interface issue.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The attack surface is the conditioning channel itself: coordinates cannot be spoofed by scene content, text bindings can; this is an architectural distinction, not a training deficiency.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 20 scenes with printed misleading labels on objects, compare a public text-prompted segmenter vs SAM box prompts.

one_line_idea: SAM's transferability to a new domain is predicted by that domain's mid-frequency spectral content: band-pass ablation shows SAM relies on a specific spatial-frequency band, and domains missing it (ultrasound speckle, low-detail thermal) fail regardless of semantic simplicity.
problem: Domain difficulty for SAM is discussed in semantic terms (unfamiliar objects) while a simpler physical account (missing spatial-frequency support the model depends on) has not been tested, though it would yield a five-minute transferability screening.
core_hypothesis: SAM's grouping decisions depend disproportionately on a mid-frequency band (measurable by band-stop performance ablation on natural images), and zero-shot performance across domains correlates strongly with target-domain energy in that band, better than with semantic-distance measures.
falsifiable_prediction: Band-stop filtering of specific frequencies degrades SAM on natural images far more than equal-energy removal elsewhere; across 10 domains, band-energy overlap predicts zero-shot rank order with high correlation, beating an embedding-distance baseline.
why_important: A physical, computable predictor of transfer beats vague domain-gap talk, guides preprocessing (frequency reshaping as cheap adaptation), and characterizes what evidence SAM's grouping actually uses.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: frequency analyses exist for classifiers; a frequency-reliance profile for promptable segmentation used as a transfer predictor appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Frequency-ablation battery on natural images to map reliance; correlate domain band-energy with zero-shot scores across a domain suite; falsified if reliance is flat or correlation is weak.
main_risk: Frequency reliance may be resolution-confounded (idea 010); analyses must normalize object scale.
community_default_belief: Domain difficulty is about semantic and textural unfamiliarity; spectral composition is a low-level detail models of this scale abstract away.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary evidence is physically carried by specific frequency bands; a model optimized for boundary acuity plausibly specialized to the bands where its training data carried boundary information.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: three band-stop conditions on 100 natural images; a sharp reliance peak is the entry result.

one_line_idea: SAM flips inconsistently between modal (visible-region) and amodal (completed-object) segmentation depending on prompt position relative to an occluder, an unacknowledged mode ambiguity that makes its outputs unreliable as either kind of ground truth.
problem: Pipelines assume SAM outputs visible-region masks; occasionally it completes objects behind occluders, and when it does is undocumented, contaminating datasets built with SAM assistance with an unlabeled mixture of modal and amodal masks.
core_hypothesis: The modal-amodal choice is governed lawfully by prompt geometry (distance from the occlusion boundary, prompted side) and occluder characteristics (thin occluders trigger completion, thick ones do not), reflecting mixed conventions in SA-1B annotation rather than randomness.
falsifiable_prediction: On a controlled occlusion battery, the completion rate varies systematically with occluder width and prompt-to-occluder distance, is stable across images with matched geometry, and matches the mixture one would predict from plausible annotation conventions (wires and poles completed, walls not).
why_important: Whoever documents the mode-selection law can both audit existing SAM-derived datasets for mixture contamination and give practitioners a control knob (prompt placement) for selecting the intended mode.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: amodal segmentation is its own subfield, but SAM's implicit mode-mixing law and its dataset-contamination consequence appear undescribed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 300 occlusion scenes parameterized by occluder width and prompt placement, measure completion rates, fit the geometric law; falsified if completion is rare or unpredictable.
main_risk: Ground truth for intended mode is a convention choice; the study must report both modal and amodal scoring throughout.
community_default_belief: SAM segments visible regions; amodal completion is out of scope and does not occur.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SA-1B annotators inevitably handled thin-occluder cases inconsistently (annotating the whole road sign behind a wire), so the model learned a context-dependent mixture, not a single convention.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 20 scenes with a thin pole crossing objects, click both sides at varying distances, tally completion behavior.

one_line_idea: Distillation kills ambiguity first: efficient SAM students match teacher mIoU while losing most of the teacher's hypothesis-space structure (multimask diversity, granularity control), because distillation targets the argmax mask, not the distribution over valid masks.
problem: Efficient SAM variants are certified by accuracy parity, and the community concludes they are drop-in replacements; if the compressed models have silently lost the ability to represent alternative segmentations, interactive and ambiguity-dependent applications inherit an untracked regression.
core_hypothesis: Standard distillation objectives (matching final masks or single embeddings) provide no gradient signal for hypothesis diversity, so student models exhibit collapsed multimask outputs and weakened prompt-granularity response even when their top-mask accuracy matches the teacher.
falsifiable_prediction: Across public efficient variants (MobileSAM-class, FastSAM-class, EfficientSAM-class), an ambiguity battery (inter-mask diversity, granularity switching under prompt sweeps, oracle-vs-top1 gap) shows large losses relative to teachers despite near-parity mIoU, with loss magnitude ordered by how output-centric each distillation objective was.
why_important: It exposes a blind spot in how model compression is certified, defines the missing evaluation, and motivates diversity-preserving distillation objectives for any multi-hypothesis model.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: efficient SAM papers report accuracy and speed; a systematic ambiguity audit across the efficiency family appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the ambiguity battery on three efficient variants and their teachers over 500 images; falsified if students preserve ambiguity structure at accuracy parity.
main_risk: Some efficient variants changed architecture (single-mask heads) making the comparison partly definitional; the audit must separate architectural removal from distillation-induced collapse.
community_default_belief: Efficient SAM variants are functionally equivalent, cheaper SAMs; accuracy parity certifies equivalence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Equivalence was only ever measured on the axis distillation optimized; unmeasured capabilities have no reason to survive compression, and ambiguity is exactly the unmeasured axis.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: one efficient variant vs teacher, inter-mask diversity and a 10-object granularity sweep; a visible collapse settles the existence question.

one_line_idea: Distilled students fail on a strict superset of teacher failures: compression does not trade failure regions but nests them, so teacher-side failure prediction transfers to students for free, enabling cheap cascade designs.
problem: Cascade systems (cheap student first, expensive teacher fallback) need to know whether student failures are predictable from teacher behavior; if failure sets are nested rather than disjoint, fallback logic and audit tooling simplify dramatically, but nobody has tested the set relationship.
core_hypothesis: Because students are optimized to imitate teachers (not to solve the task independently), student competence is approximately teacher competence intersected with capacity constraints, predicting per-instance failure containment: cases the teacher fails, the student fails too, plus additional capacity-driven failures.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-instance evaluation of teacher-student pairs shows the student succeeding where the teacher fails at rates far below what independent errors at matched marginal accuracy would predict (containment violation rate close to noise), consistently across distilled variants but not across independently-trained model pairs.
why_important: Containment (or its refutation) determines correct cascade and ensemble design for the SAM family, and it tests a basic proposition about what imitation learning can and cannot add.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: teacher-student agreement is studied via aggregate fidelity; the set-relationship (containment) framing with cascade implications appears new for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Per-instance success matrices for three teacher-student pairs plus an independently-trained control pair on 2000 instances; falsified if students beat teachers on a substantial instance fraction.
main_risk: Instance-level success requires choosing IoU thresholds; results should be shown threshold-robust.
community_default_belief: Students trade accuracy for speed diffusely; where they fail relative to the teacher is idiosyncratic.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Imitation objectives upper-bound student knowledge by teacher outputs on the training distribution; novel student successes would require information the training signal never carried, making containment the structural default.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: one pair, 300 instances, count student-succeeds-teacher-fails cases against the independence baseline.

one_line_idea: Feature-space distillation preserves prompt responsiveness while output-space distillation destroys it: two certified-equivalent compression routes produce behaviorally different interactive models, and the difference is invisible to standard benchmarks.
problem: Distillation recipes for SAM differ in what they match (encoder embeddings vs final masks), and recipe choice is treated as an implementation detail; if it determines interactive behavior, the community needs to know before efficient variants become the default annotation backends.
core_hypothesis: Matching encoder features transfers the representation the decoder's prompt machinery was calibrated for, preserving click-response dynamics; matching final masks lets the student solve the imitation task with prompt-insensitive shortcuts, so interactive responsiveness (marginal effect of each additional click) degrades specifically under output-space distillation.
falsifiable_prediction: Students distilled with feature matching show click-response curves close to the teacher, while output-matched students at equal single-shot accuracy show flattened curves (later clicks change masks less), with the difference persisting across student capacities.
why_important: It provides a causal design rule for compressing interactive models (match the interface-feeding representation, not the behavior), applicable beyond segmentation to any prompt-conditioned system.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: both distillation styles exist in the efficient-SAM family; attributing interactive-behavior differences to the matching target with controlled experiments appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Distill matched-capacity students under both objectives from the same teacher and data, compare click-response curves and clicks-to-quality; falsified if behavior is equivalent.
main_risk: Fair capacity and schedule matching between distillation styles is delicate; multiple budgets needed.
community_default_belief: What matters in distillation is student capacity and data; the choice of matching target is secondary once accuracy is matched.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Accuracy is a single functional of behavior; different matching targets can produce equal accuracy with different function classes, and only the feature-matched class is constrained to preserve the prompt interface's operating conditions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: two small students (one per objective) on a modest corpus, click-response comparison on 100 objects.

one_line_idea: Quantization is prompt-type biased: INT8 SAM loses point-prompt accuracy well before box-prompt accuracy, because sparse point information rides small activations that quantization noise drowns, making current quantization certifications misleading for interactive use.
problem: Quantized SAMs are validated on aggregate accuracy, typically with box prompts (from detection pipelines); if the prompt types degrade at different quantization levels, edge deployments optimized for interactive clicking are certified with the wrong test.
core_hypothesis: Point prompts inject low-magnitude, spatially-sparse signals into the decoder whose downstream computation operates near quantization noise floors, whereas box prompts inject redundant, higher-magnitude constraints; therefore accuracy-vs-bitwidth curves diverge by prompt type, with points collapsing one to two bits earlier.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping quantization levels shows a consistent prompt-type gap in degradation onset, localized (by per-layer sensitivity analysis) to decoder cross-attention paths carrying prompt-token information rather than to the encoder.
why_important: Prompt-conditional fragility under quantization redefines how promptable models must be certified for edge deployment and identifies which layers need mixed-precision protection, a directly actionable engineering result.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: quantization studies of SAM exist for aggregate accuracy; prompt-type-stratified quantization analysis appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Quantize SAM at four bitwidths, evaluate point vs box protocols on matched instances, run per-layer sensitivity attribution; falsified if degradation is prompt-independent.
main_risk: Results may vary across quantization schemes (PTQ vs QAT); a scheme grid inflates cost but is needed for generality.
community_default_belief: Quantization degrades models uniformly across usage modes; one accuracy number per bitwidth characterizes the trade-off.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Uniform degradation assumes signal magnitudes are homogeneous across pathways, which is false by construction in an architecture mixing dense image evidence with sparse prompt tokens.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: one INT8 conversion, points vs boxes on 200 instances; a visible asymmetric drop is the entry evidence.

one_line_idea: Token merging and pruning for SAM encoders selectively destroys thin and small structures long before average metrics move, because merging criteria based on feature similarity preferentially eliminate the minority tokens carrying rare-structure evidence.
problem: Token-reduction methods are adopted for speed with average-accuracy validation, but dense prediction needs every spatial location; if reduction is structurally biased against exactly the hard structures (vessels, wires, cracks), efficiency work is quietly re-introducing failure modes adaptation work just fixed.
core_hypothesis: Feature-similarity-based token merging removes tokens belonging to spatially-small, texturally-distinct structures first (they have few similar neighbors and low total attention mass), so structure-stratified accuracy degrades ordered by structure thinness while global mIoU is flat, and a structure-aware merge criterion eliminates the bias at equal speedup.
falsifiable_prediction: Applying standard token merging at increasing reduction ratios shows thin-structure metrics collapsing at ratios where overall mIoU changes marginally; instrumenting merge decisions confirms disproportionate merging of thin-structure tokens; a protected-token variant restores their accuracy at matched throughput.
why_important: It documents a systematic efficiency-fairness trade-off across structure types and provides the fix, keeping efficient SAMs usable in the industrial and scientific domains most sensitive to thin structures.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: token merging (e.g., ToMe) is established for classification ViTs; structure-stratified consequences for promptable dense prediction and a protective criterion appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Token-merging sweep on SAM across reduction ratios, structure-stratified evaluation on natural plus thin-structure datasets, merge-decision audit, and one protected-merge arm; falsified if degradation is structure-uniform.
main_risk: The protected criterion could reintroduce compute overhead that eats the speedup; throughput must be honestly matched.
community_default_belief: Token reduction with flat average-metric curves is safe to deploy; degradation, when it comes, is gradual and uniform.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Merging criteria are majority-statistics driven by design; rare-structure evidence is definitionally minority statistics, so the bias is baked into the mechanism and invisible to average metrics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: one merging config at two ratios on a vessel-like dataset plus COCO; compare metric-drop ratios between the two.

one_line_idea: The IoU head is a free adapter router: selecting which domain LoRA to apply per image by comparing SAM's own predicted-score distributions under each adapter beats both single adapters and weight merging, with zero additional trained parameters.
problem: Multi-domain deployments must choose among adapter selection (needs a trained router), merging (loses per-domain performance), or manual routing (operational burden); an intrinsic routing signal would eliminate the extra machinery, but nobody has checked whether the model already provides one.
core_hypothesis: Running a probe prompt set through each candidate adapter and reading the predicted-score distribution yields a competence signal sufficient for near-oracle adapter selection, because the score head (though miscalibrated absolutely, idea 023) remains relatively informative across adapters on the same image.
falsifiable_prediction: Score-based routing achieves a large fraction of oracle-routing accuracy across a five-domain adapter zoo, beating the best single adapter and uniform merging, and degrades gracefully as domains become similar (where routing errors are harmless).
why_important: Zero-cost routing makes adapter zoos operationally simple, and relative-competence readout from self-assessment heads would be a reusable pattern for foundation-model ecosystems generally.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: adapter routing via trained gates exists; routing via the frozen model's own quality head appears untested for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Five domain adapters, mixed-domain test stream, compare score-routing vs oracle vs best-single vs merged; falsified if score-routing tracks the merged or single baselines.
main_risk: Idea 023's style-critic effect could make scores uninformative exactly on hard out-of-domain images, capping routing quality; the two studies should share infrastructure.
community_default_belief: Routing among adapters requires training a router or gating network; internal heads are too unreliable under shift to drive selection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Absolute calibration and relative discrimination are different properties; a head can be biased yet still rank its own competence across adapters usefully, and only absolute calibration has been criticized.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: two adapters, two domains, route by mean top-score over a 3x3 probe grid; compare to oracle routing on 100 images.

one_line_idea: Catastrophic remembering: narrow-domain PEFT resurrects pretraining biases that SAM's final training had suppressed (texture leakage, compact-mask preference), so adaptation can move a model backward along its own training history, not just away from it.
problem: Forgetting is framed as losing recent capabilities; the possibility that fine-tuning reactivates older, suppressed behaviors (because narrow data removes the pressure that suppressed them) is unexamined for segmentation models, yet it predicts a specific, testable error signature.
core_hypothesis: Behaviors suppressed late in SAM's training (errors characteristic of MAE-stage or early-data-engine-stage models) reappear under narrow-domain PEFT in proportion to how far the adaptation data distribution is from the data that drove the suppression, producing error profiles that match earlier-stage models more than a generic degradation model would predict.
falsifiable_prediction: Error-profile similarity between adapted SAM and reference earlier-stage models (MAE probes, weaker segmenters) increases with adaptation, on non-target images, beyond what matched-accuracy random degradation controls show.
why_important: If adaptation moves models backward along their developmental trajectory, adapter safety evaluation should include regression tests against known ancestral failure modes, a fundamentally different test battery than current practice.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: the reactivation-of-suppressed-behavior framing exists in psychology; a quantitative version for foundation-model adaptation appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define an ancestral-error battery from MAE-feature probes and early open segmenters, track adapted-SAM similarity to it across PEFT intensity with degradation-matched controls; falsified if adapted errors are no more ancestral than random degradation.
main_risk: Constructing credible ancestral references is the weak point; MAE probes are an approximation of SAM's actual early stages.
community_default_belief: Fine-tuning damage is forward-looking noise: the model gets worse in unpredictable ways, not in historically-structured ways.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Suppression in neural networks is often implemented as context-dependent overrides rather than erasure; remove the maintaining pressure and the override decays first, un-masking the old behavior — a mechanism with support in continual-learning analyses of smaller models.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: heavy LoRA on one narrow domain, compare error-type histogram on natural images against frozen SAM and an MAE-probe baseline.

one_line_idea: Interference between simultaneously-composed LoRAs is predicted by principal angles between their update subspaces: a five-minute weight-space measurement forecasts whether two adapters can be stacked, replacing trial-and-error composition.
problem: Users increasingly stack adapters (domain plus task plus style), discovering incompatibilities empirically after deployment; a predictive compatibility metric computable from weights alone would make composition an engineering discipline instead of alchemy.
core_hypothesis: Destructive interference between composed LoRAs is driven by subspace overlap in specific layers (aligned directions with conflicting scalings), so a weighted principal-angle profile predicts composed-model performance drop, and orthogonality-encouraged retraining of one adapter eliminates the interference it predicts.
falsifiable_prediction: Across an adapter-pair grid, the subspace-overlap metric correlates strongly with measured composition damage; pairs retrained with orthogonality constraints show both reduced predicted overlap and reduced actual damage, closing the causal loop.
why_important: Composability is the core promise of the adapter ecosystem; a validated predictor plus a constructive fix would be immediately adopted and would ground composition in measurable weight geometry.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: LoRA merging and interference are actively studied in NLP; a validated per-layer principal-angle predictor with a causal retraining arm for segmentation adapters appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train eight single-purpose adapters on SAM, evaluate all pairs composed, correlate damage with subspace metrics, run the orthogonal-retraining arm on the worst pairs; falsified if geometry does not predict damage.
main_risk: Interference may be dominated by activation-space (data-dependent) effects invisible to weight-space geometry, which the study design should detect via residual analysis.
community_default_belief: Adapter compatibility must be discovered empirically per combination; weight inspection cannot tell you whether behaviors will conflict.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-rank updates live in small subspaces where geometric collision is well-defined and rare by chance; when collisions do occur they are plausibly both necessary and sufficient for conflict, making prediction feasible precisely because of the low-rank structure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: three adapter pairs spanning low to high subspace overlap, measure composition damage, check ordering.

evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK: LoRA composition and merging are studied in the NLP literature; the segmentation-specific predictive law is MODEL SPECULATION

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept but flagged: subspace-angle predictor is a concrete pre-composition measurement tool; verify against adapter-merging prior art before Stage 2.

one_line_idea: Domain shifts share low-rank structure: one shared LoRA trained jointly on N diverse domains matches N separate LoRAs at one-Nth the parameters, implying that adaptation learns a common shift-correction operator rather than N unrelated fixes.
problem: The adapter-per-domain paradigm assumes domain corrections are essentially unrelated; if a shared low-rank correction captures most of every domain's gain, the field is storing and serving N copies of nearly the same function while missing the scientific point that domain gap has universal structure.
core_hypothesis: A large component of what each domain LoRA learns is a domain-generic correction (e.g., re-weighting frequency bands, relaxing photometric priors, adjusting decoder thresholds) so joint training finds it with minimal per-domain residual, and the shared update's singular vectors are interpretable as generic shift operators.
falsifiable_prediction: Shared LoRA at rank r approaches the average performance of per-domain LoRAs at rank r each, the gap shrinking as domain count grows; SVD of per-domain updates independently trained shows high pairwise subspace overlap in specific layers, corroborating shared structure.
why_important: Both an infrastructure result (one adapter to serve all) and a scientific one: it would mean domain gap for a segmentation foundation model is a low-dimensional, characterizable object, not an unstructured catch-all.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: multi-task adapters exist; the claim that cross-domain segmentation shift itself is low-rank-shared, with the SVD-overlap corroboration, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Six domains: per-domain vs shared LoRA at matched total and per-domain parameters, plus subspace-overlap analysis of independent updates; falsified if shared lags badly and overlaps are near chance.
main_risk: Negative transfer between conflicting domains could mask shared structure; per-domain residual mini-adapters should be an arm to separate the effects.
community_default_belief: Each domain needs its own adapter; domain corrections do not meaningfully share structure across dissimilar domains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: All these domains deviate from the same pretraining distribution, so their corrections all point back toward relaxing the same priors — a common component the per-domain paradigm never looks for.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: SVD-overlap analysis of three existing per-domain LoRAs; high overlap justifies the joint-training experiment.

one_line_idea: Self-training SAM on its own confident masks converges to degenerate over-smooth segmentation because the confidence signal is style-biased (idea 023): the obvious test-time adaptation baseline is predicted to fail in a specific, diagnosable way.
problem: Test-time adaptation via confident pseudo-labels is the default recipe ported from classification; for SAM, if confidence tracks mask style rather than correctness, self-training amplifies the style prior each round, and the failure will be misread as a data problem rather than a mechanism problem.
core_hypothesis: Iterative self-training with score-thresholded pseudo-masks drifts the model toward producing compact, smooth masks regardless of image evidence, with measurable shrinkage of boundary complexity distribution across rounds, while true accuracy first plateaus then declines — a signature distinguishable from ordinary overfitting.
falsifiable_prediction: Across self-training rounds, predicted-score-selected masks show monotonically decreasing boundary complexity, the model's outputs on held-out images follow, and accuracy on complex-boundary objects declines before accuracy on compact objects, exactly the ordering the style-bias mechanism predicts and ordinary overfitting does not.
why_important: It preempts a wave of flawed test-time adaptation work by identifying the failure mechanism in advance, and the diagnostic signature (complexity shrinkage ordering) lets others check their own pipelines cheaply.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: self-training failure modes are known generically (confirmation bias); the style-collapse mechanism specific to mask-quality-scored segmentation appears unarticulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run score-thresholded self-training on two shifted domains for five rounds, track complexity distributions and stratified accuracy; falsified if outputs do not drift toward compactness or the decline ordering is absent.
main_risk: Well-chosen regularizers might mask the effect; the study should include both vanilla and regularized arms to map when the failure is expressed.
community_default_belief: Confidence-filtered self-training is a reasonable, usually-helpful adaptation baseline; failures come from too-low thresholds or too-few iterations.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The recipe assumes confidence correlates with correctness under shift, which idea 023 argues is precisely what breaks; recycling a biased critic as a teacher institutionalizes its bias.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: two self-training rounds on one domain, compare boundary-complexity histograms of selected pseudo-labels round over round; visible shrinkage is the mechanism's fingerprint.

one_line_idea: Click-policy shift is a hidden domain gap: SAM was trained on simulator clicks (error-region centers), humans click salient interiors and high-contrast landmarks, and this policy mismatch accounts for a measurable slice of real-world underperformance relative to benchmarks.
problem: The gap between benchmark and deployed interactive performance is attributed to image domain shift, but the prompts themselves are also out-of-distribution: no one has quantified how much performance is lost purely because human click distributions differ from training simulators.
core_hypothesis: SAM's interactive competence is calibrated to simulator click statistics, so evaluating with human-logged clicks on in-domain images (no image shift at all) already produces a significant performance drop, and retraining the click simulator to match human statistics closes most of that drop.
falsifiable_prediction: On identical images, human-click evaluation underperforms simulator-click evaluation by a margin exceeding annotator noise, the margin correlates with per-image divergence between human and simulator click distributions, and a human-statistics-matched fine-tune recovers most of it without any image-domain data.
why_important: It cleanly separates two conflated sources of deployment gap and shows that prompt-distribution alignment is a data-free adaptation axis — likely cheaper than any image-domain adaptation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: click simulation strategies are studied for training efficiency; framing human-vs-simulator click divergence as a quantifiable domain gap with its own adaptation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect human clicks on 500 benchmark objects, evaluate frozen SAM under both click sources, then fine-tune with human-matched simulation and re-evaluate; falsified if the two click sources perform equally.
main_risk: Human click collection is a small user study with IRB-style overhead; public annotation-tool logs could substitute if accessible.
community_default_belief: Clicks are clicks; performance gaps in deployment come from image distribution shift, not from who or what generated the click.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The model's conditional distribution was fit to a specific prompt-generating process; conditioning variables are part of the data distribution, and changing their statistics is textbook covariate shift that happens to be invisible in image-space audits.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 50 objects, five self-collected human clicks each vs standard simulator clicks, paired accuracy comparison on frozen SAM.

evidence_label.prior_work_basis: KNOWN FACT: SAM's interactive training used simulated prompts per the paper; human-divergence magnitude is HYPOTHESIS pending measurement

one_line_idea: Interactive correction has oscillation modes: correcting one region creates errors elsewhere with probability that grows with adaptation strength, so heavily adapted SAMs exhibit whack-a-mole dynamics that make some targets uncorrectable in finite clicks.
problem: Interactive evaluation assumes monotone convergence to the target mask; if the correction operator has oscillatory or divergent modes (fixing A breaks B, fixing B re-breaks A), click-count metrics hide a qualitative failure class that determines whether annotation tasks can complete at all.
core_hypothesis: The correction map (current mask plus corrective click to next mask) is a learned operator whose contraction property is not guaranteed; PEFT that strengthens domain priors reduces contraction (the model keeps snapping back to its prior), increasing the rate of non-converging correction sequences measurable as limit cycles in mask space.
falsifiable_prediction: Simulated correction runs show a nonzero and adaptation-strength-increasing rate of cyclic or non-converging sequences (mask trajectory revisits previous states within a tolerance), concentrated on objects conflicting with the adapted prior; frozen SAM shows the lowest cycle rate.
why_important: Convergence of interactive correction is the property annotation economics actually depends on; characterizing and monitoring the correction operator's dynamics introduces a control-theoretic lens on interactive segmentation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: clicks-to-quality is standard; treating interactive refinement as a dynamical system and measuring its convergence and cycles appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run scripted 20-click correction policies on 500 objects across frozen and adapted checkpoints, detect cycles and non-convergence, correlate rates with adaptation strength; falsified if trajectories converge monotonically everywhere.
main_risk: Cycle detection depends on the correction policy; several policies must be tested to show the phenomenon is model-driven, not policy-driven.
community_default_belief: More corrective clicks monotonically approach the target; interactive refinement always terminates for a competent user.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Each correction is a full re-inference through a model with strong priors, not an incremental edit; there is no architectural guarantee of contraction, and strengthened priors actively oppose corrections toward prior-inconsistent targets.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 30 prior-conflicting objects (unusual shapes in an adapted domain), 15-click scripted corrections, check for state revisits.

one_line_idea: The model's best click is not where humans click: a gradient-derived where-to-click advisor (computed from SAM's own sensitivity) increases per-click information and cuts annotation time, revealing that human click intuitions are miscalibrated to the model's actual decision geometry.
problem: Interactive tools let users click by intuition, and all guidance research focuses on improving the model; the complementary question — telling the user where their click would help the model most — is unaddressed, though it needs no model changes at all.
core_hypothesis: Per-pixel expected mask improvement (estimable from prompt-sensitivity maps or output variance under hypothetical clicks) identifies click locations substantially better than human choice, and displaying a top-k suggestion overlay improves clicks-to-quality even after accounting for user compliance costs.
falsifiable_prediction: In simulation, advisor-chosen clicks dominate human-logged clicks in marginal IoU gain per click; in a small user study, the overlay condition reduces time-to-target-quality with no accuracy loss, and the advantage is largest exactly on objects where idea 006's failure structure makes intuitive clicks bad.
why_important: It inverts the adaptation direction (adapt the human interface to the model rather than the model to data), a cheap and immediately deployable path to better annotation throughput that also maps where model and human spatial intuitions diverge.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: active-learning-style query selection exists at the image level; per-click spatial guidance derived from the model's own sensitivity for interactive segmentation appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the sensitivity-map advisor, run simulated comparisons on 1000 objects, then a 10-person user study with and without overlay; falsified if advisor clicks are no better than human or centroid baselines.
main_risk: Sensitivity estimation per candidate click is expensive; approximations (coarse grids, one forward pass surrogates) must be validated for fidelity.
community_default_belief: Humans know where to click; interactive segmentation research should improve the model's response to clicks, not redirect the human.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Human clicks optimize human-perceptual saliency, but the model's decision geometry (attention structure, failure filaments) is alien to human intuition; nothing aligns the two, and ideas 006 and 009 predict specific divergences.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: simulated advisor-vs-centroid-vs-random comparison on 200 objects; a clear per-click information gain justifies the user study.

one_line_idea: Fine-tuning on accumulated user corrections personalizes toward the user's annotation style rather than toward accuracy: correction-trained models drift measurably toward individual annotator idiosyncrasies, conflating personalization with improvement.
problem: Products increasingly fine-tune on the corrections users make (treating them as free ground truth), assuming corrections encode true errors; corrections also encode the corrector's stylistic preferences (boundary tightness, hole handling), and no evaluation separates the two learning signals.
core_hypothesis: Training on one annotator's corrections improves agreement with that annotator faster than agreement with a multi-annotator consensus, and a decomposition against consensus ground truth shows a substantial fraction of the learned update is style, predicting degraded performance when the model serves other users.
falsifiable_prediction: Correction-trained models show rising same-annotator agreement with flat or declining consensus agreement, and cross-user evaluation shows other annotators need more corrections with the personalized model than with the base model on matched tasks.
why_important: It warns that correction-loop learning silently fragments shared models into per-user dialects — an important finding for the growing human-in-the-loop adaptation industry — and defines the consensus-based evaluation such systems need.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: annotator bias is known in dataset construction; its dynamics inside online correction-based fine-tuning of a foundation segmenter appear unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multi-annotator dataset with consensus labels: fine-tune on single-annotator corrections, track same-annotator vs consensus agreement, then cross-user click-count evaluation; falsified if consensus agreement rises in step with same-annotator agreement.
main_risk: Requires multi-annotator infrastructure; annotator style differences may be small in some domains, bounding the effect.
community_default_belief: User corrections are ground truth; training on them straightforwardly improves the model for everyone.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A correction fixes the delta between model output and one person's intended mask, and intentions differ systematically across people; the training signal cannot distinguish shared truth from private style without multiple sources, which correction loops never have.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day if two-annotator data exists: fine-tune on annotator A corrections, evaluate against annotator B labels; a widening A-vs-B gap is the signature.

one_line_idea: Prompt reuse across near-duplicate images fails silently at a predictable rate: prompts transferred between adjacent video frames or repeated product shots produce degraded masks without degraded confidence, defining an unstudied reliability metric (prompt transferability) for promptable models.
problem: Batch workflows commonly reuse a prompt across visually similar images (frames, catalog shots, tiled scans) assuming near-duplicate inputs preserve prompt validity; the failure rate of this ubiquitous practice has never been characterized, and confidence does not flag it.
core_hypothesis: Prompt validity decays with small image transformations much faster than image similarity metrics suggest (because failure sets from idea 006 move with texture, not with content), so transferred prompts hit failure regions at rates predictable from local image-gradient changes but not from global similarity, while predicted scores stay high.
falsifiable_prediction: On near-duplicate pairs (consecutive frames, re-shots), reusing source-image prompts yields a measurable rate of severe mask degradation uncorrelated with predicted score, and a cheap local-gradient-change statistic around the prompt location predicts failures with useful AUROC.
why_important: It quantifies a silent failure in widespread workflows, provides a deployable guard (the local-change statistic), and introduces prompt transferability as a robustness dimension distinct from image robustness.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: robustness to image perturbation at fixed prompts is studied; robustness of a fixed prompt across naturally-varying near-duplicates appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build near-duplicate pairs from video and catalog datasets, transfer prompts, measure degradation rates and score blindness, fit the local-change predictor; falsified if transfer failures are rare or well-flagged by scores.
main_risk: Ground truth on both images of each pair is needed; annotation cost bounds the study size.
community_default_belief: If two images look almost identical, a prompt that works on one works on the other; batch prompt reuse is safe.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Prompt validity depends on the local decision geometry at the click location, which is far more sensitive to small perturbations than global appearance is; similarity metrics measure the wrong thing for this purpose.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: 50 consecutive-frame pairs, transfer clicks, count severe degradations and check score behavior on failures.

one_line_idea: Resolution adaptation is a positional-encoding problem, not a feature problem: tuning only SAM's positional embeddings (all other weights frozen) recovers most of the gain that high-resolution fine-tuning provides, isolating where resolution knowledge lives.
problem: Adapting SAM to higher-resolution inputs is done by expensive full or encoder fine-tuning, on the assumption that features must re-learn scale; if interpolated positional embeddings are the actual bottleneck, resolution transfer costs a thousand parameters, and the community misunderstands what breaks under resolution change.
core_hypothesis: Feature computations (attention patterns, local mixing) are largely scale-covariant, and the dominant failure at unseen resolutions comes from positional-embedding interpolation distorting spatial geometry; therefore PE-only tuning at the target resolution closes most of the gap to full high-res fine-tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: At doubled input resolution, PE-only tuning recovers a large majority of the full-fine-tuning improvement across datasets, and attention-pattern analysis confirms pre-tuning distortions concentrate at positions where interpolation error is largest.
why_important: It reduces an expensive adaptation to a trivial one and answers a representational question — whether scale handling in ViT segmenters is encoded in weights or in the positional scaffold — with consequences for all high-resolution dense prediction.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: PE interpolation tricks are folklore; a controlled decomposition attributing resolution-transfer gains to PE-only adaptation for promptable segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three arms at high resolution (frozen with interpolated PE, PE-only tuned, full fine-tune) on two datasets; falsified if PE-only tuning recovers little of the full-fine-tune gain.
main_risk: Memory costs of high-resolution attention may force windowing changes that confound the attribution.
community_default_belief: Resolution transfer requires adapting features; positional-embedding interpolation is a lossless technicality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention is position-blind except through the PEs, so resolution change enters the computation almost entirely through the positional scaffold — the one component everyone treats as a detail.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: PE-only tuning at 2x resolution on one dataset vs frozen-interpolated baseline; the recovered fraction is immediately informative.

evidence_label.prior_work_basis: KNOWN FACT: ViTs require positional-embedding interpolation at new resolutions; attribution claim is MODEL SPECULATION

one_line_idea: PEFT under a fixed prompt protocol turns SAM into a prompt-ignoring semantic segmenter: adapted models' outputs become nearly invariant to prompt content, meaning many published adapted-SAM results are really measuring a learned semantic prior wearing a promptable interface.
problem: Adaptation pipelines train and evaluate with rigid prompt protocols (always a centroid click or a ground-truth box), so nothing in the objective requires continued prompt sensitivity; the field may be publishing promptable-model results that a prompt-free model would replicate, without anyone measuring prompt dependence post-adaptation.
core_hypothesis: Prompt-ablation sensitivity (output change when the prompt is moved, degraded, or randomized) collapses during protocol-rigid PEFT at a rate driven by target-dataset homogeneity, and adapted models approach the behavior of an equivalent prompt-free segmentation head trained on the same data.
falsifiable_prediction: Post-PEFT models show drastically reduced output variance under prompt randomization compared to frozen SAM, their accuracy with random prompts approaches their accuracy with correct prompts on the target domain, and a prompt-free distilled head matches them, none of which holds for frozen SAM.
why_important: It changes the interpretation of a large experimental literature (what was actually evaluated), and defines prompt-dependence retention as a mandatory reported metric for adapted promptable models.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: prompt-sensitivity collapse under rigid-protocol adaptation is a natural consequence nobody appears to have quantified or named.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take five published-style adaptation recipes, measure prompt-randomization sensitivity before and after training, plus the prompt-free-equivalent comparison; falsified if sensitivity survives adaptation broadly.
main_risk: Some target tasks genuinely have one object per image, where prompt invariance is arguably correct behavior; the study must include multi-object target domains where invariance is unambiguously pathological.
community_default_belief: An adapted SAM is still a promptable model; the prompt keeps doing its job after fine-tuning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optimization removes whatever the loss does not require, and rigid protocols make prompt information redundant with the dataset prior; the interface remains, the function behind it quietly changes category.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hours: one public adapted checkpoint, compare masks under correct vs random prompts on its target data; near-identical outputs are the smoking gun.

one_line_idea: For non-RGB modalities, a tiny learned input stem beats the standard channel-inflation trick: freezing all of SAM and learning only a 1x1 modality-to-pseudo-RGB projection outperforms replicating RGB weights across channels, showing the modality gap lives at the input interface.
problem: Depth, thermal, SAR, and multispectral imagery are wrestled into SAM by copying RGB patch-embedding weights across channels or naive grayscale conversion, a convention adopted without comparison against the minimal alternative of learning the input projection itself.
core_hypothesis: SAM's features are modality-agnostic once inputs are mapped into the photometric statistics it expects, so a learned input stem of a few thousand parameters (with everything else frozen) captures most of what encoder PEFT achieves on non-RGB modalities, while channel inflation misaligns input statistics and forces downstream layers to compensate.
falsifiable_prediction: Across three non-RGB modalities, stem-only training beats channel inflation consistently and reaches a large fraction of encoder-LoRA performance, and the learned stems converge to interpretable mappings (e.g., depth gradients to pseudo-shading) across seeds.
why_important: A validated minimal recipe would immediately serve several application communities, and the interpretable-stem finding would show that cross-modality transfer of segmentation features is an input-coding problem rather than a representation problem.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: learned input adapters exist in scattered forms; a controlled stem-vs-inflation-vs-LoRA comparison with stem interpretability analysis for SAM appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three modalities, three arms (inflation, stem-only, encoder LoRA) at matched data; compare accuracy and analyze stem weights across seeds; falsified if stems lag inflation or LoRA dominates by wide margins everywhere.
main_risk: Modalities with fundamentally different noise physics (speckle in SAR) may defeat any pointwise input mapping, bounding the claim's scope.
community_default_belief: Channel inflation or grayscale replication is the standard, adequate way to feed non-RGB data to RGB-pretrained models; real gains require adapting the encoder.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Inflation preserves weights but not input statistics, feeding the frozen encoder data far off its expected manifold; a learned stem fixes the manifold mismatch directly at the cheapest possible location.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: depth modality, stem-only vs inflation with frozen SAM on one dataset; the gap direction is immediately informative.

one_line_idea: Loss choice shapes mask topology more than architecture choice: the focal-plus-dice convention in SAM adaptation imposes a measurable bias toward simply-connected masks, an ignored confound that may explain topology-related conclusions across the PEFT literature.
problem: Adaptation papers vary architectures and PEFT methods while uniformly copying the loss recipe, so systematic topology effects of the loss (hole-filling, fragment suppression) are invisible in comparisons and get misattributed to methods or domains.
core_hypothesis: Dice-family losses, by rewarding bulk overlap, penalize topologically complex predictions asymmetrically, so models adapted with focal-dice produce fewer holes and fragments than boundary- or cross-entropy-trained counterparts at matched IoU, and reported method differences in topology-sensitive domains shrink substantially once loss is controlled.
falsifiable_prediction: A loss-by-method factorial on topology-rich domains shows loss main effects on topology metrics (Betti-number error, hole recall) exceeding method main effects, while IoU differences remain method-dominated, demonstrating that topology conclusions in the literature track the loss convention.
why_important: Identifying a field-wide confound redirects credit assignment in dozens of comparisons and gives topology-sensitive application areas (medical, industrial inspection) a cheap corrective: change the loss, not the architecture.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: loss effects on segmentation topology are known in principle; quantifying loss-vs-method effect ratios as a confound audit of the SAM-adaptation literature appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two domains rich in holes and fragments, three losses crossed with three PEFT methods, topology-decomposed evaluation; falsified if method effects dominate topology metrics.
main_risk: Interaction effects (loss-method) could complicate the clean main-effect story; the factorial design handles but complicates messaging.
community_default_belief: The loss recipe is settled infrastructure; differences between adapted models reflect their adaptation methods.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Losses define what error structure is cheap; topology is exactly the mask property over which common losses differ most, yet it is the property comparisons never stratify by.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: one method, two losses, one hole-rich dataset; a topology-metric gap at matched IoU demonstrates the confound exists.

one_line_idea: Pseudo-label bias amplification law: students trained on SAM everything-mode outputs inherit its anti-small, anti-thin biases amplified by a measurable factor, so each generation of SAM-labeled training data drifts further from reality in a predictable direction.
problem: SAM-generated pseudo-labels now feed countless training pipelines; if the generator's known biases are amplified (not just copied) by students — because students turn soft, occasional omissions into confident systematic ones — the ecosystem is compounding a directional error nobody is tracking across generations.
core_hypothesis: Bias amplification through pseudo-label training holds for segmentation: the student's size-dependent recall curve is a sharpened version of the teacher's (omission probabilities pushed toward 0 or 1), and a second generation (student labels training a new student) sharpens further, following a contraction map whose fixed point excludes small structures entirely.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring size-stratified recall across teacher, student, and second-generation student shows monotone steepening of the size-recall curve at its low end, with amplification factors consistent across architectures, and simple label-noise corrections (loss reweighting by teacher uncertainty) break the contraction.
why_important: It quantifies a compounding ecosystem-level risk of foundation-model-generated data, gives the field an early-warning metric (curve steepening), and connects to bias-amplification results known from classification.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS: bias amplification is documented for attribute classification; a generational contraction analysis for segmentation pseudo-labels with an intervention appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate SAM pseudo-labels on a corpus with real ground truth available, train a student, generate second-generation labels, train again; compare size-stratified recall curves across generations; falsified if curves do not steepen.
main_risk: Two generations of training is compute-heavy; small architectures and subsampled corpora keep it tractable at the cost of scale realism.
community_default_belief: Students average out teacher noise; pseudo-label training approximately preserves the teacher's quality profile rather than amplifying its biases.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging holds for symmetric noise, but omission of small structures is asymmetric systematic bias; students fit the systematic component and, facing consistent absence, learn confident absence — the amplification mechanism.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day: one generation only — compare teacher vs student size-recall curves on ground-truthed data; visible steepening at generation one is the core signal.

one_line_idea: Binary masks are a category error for smoke: segmentation error concentrates in a penumbra band that tracks optical thickness, not annotation noise.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Smoke is a volumetric participating medium with no material surface, yet dense-prediction benchmarks represent it with binary masks that assert a crisp spatial extent. [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant error source in smoke segmentation may be representational (forcing a boundary where none exists) rather than perceptual (failing to see the smoke).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-pixel disagreement between any trained model and its ground truth is a monotonic function of local optical transmittance: errors concentrate where transmittance is intermediate, and this dependence persists across architectures because it is a property of the label representation, not the model.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] On synthetic smoke renders with known per-pixel transmittance, plotting model-vs-label disagreement against transmittance will show a sharp unimodal peak at intermediate transmittance for every architecture tested; if disagreement is instead flat or architecture-specific, the hypothesis is false.
why_important: If most residual error is representational, the field's effort on bigger backbones for smoke/fire segmentation is misdirected, and the fix is changing the output space (scalar transmittance fields), which is cheap by comparison.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Soft matting for smoke exists, but a systematic architecture-independent attribution of error to the binary representation itself, using physically known transmittance as the controlled variable, may not have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render a small synthetic smoke dataset with ground-truth density (any volumetric renderer), threshold density at a fixed level to create binary labels, train two or three standard segmentation models, and regress per-pixel error against known transmittance.
main_risk: Synthetic smoke may not transfer: the error-vs-transmittance relationship could be an artifact of the renderer rather than a property of real smoke imagery.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Smoke segmentation is treated as a standard hard segmentation task where better features and more data will close the gap to crisp-object performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotator thresholds may be consistent enough that the binary representation is effectively well-defined, making the penumbra error a small, bounded term rather than the dominant one.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take any pretrained smoke or general segmentation model, run it on a handful of synthetic renders with known transmittance, and check within a day whether the error histogram concentrates at intermediate transmittance.
