one_line_idea: Fire segmentation may depend on sensor saturation: HDR imagery without clipped pixels could break current models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Flames commonly saturate consumer sensors, producing clipped white-yellow regions. [HYPOTHESIS] Models may have learned saturation artifacts (clipping plateaus, blooming) as the primary fire cue, which would fail on HDR or properly exposed professional footage precisely in high-stakes monitoring deployments.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Fire segmentation performance drops disproportionately on unclipped renditions of the same scenes (HDR tone mappings preserving flame texture), and the learned models' most salient features localize on clipping boundaries rather than combustion structure, establishing saturation as a load-bearing shortcut.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Paired clipped versus unclipped renditions will show a large performance asymmetry and attribution maps concentrated on clipping artifacts; parity across renditions falsifies the saturation-shortcut claim.
why_important: Professional fire-monitoring cameras increasingly avoid clipping; a saturation dependence would mean models validated on consumer footage silently fail on the better sensors used in deployment.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Exposure robustness is studied broadly; identifying sensor clipping as the specific learned cue for fire may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture or synthesize HDR fire scenes, produce clipped and unclipped low-dynamic-range renditions, evaluate models on both, and run attribution analysis on the difference.
main_risk: Tone-mapping choices introduce their own distribution shift, which must be controlled with non-fire scenes.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Fire is assumed easy because of distinctive color; sensor pipeline effects are ignored in the fire-segmentation literature I am aware of (unverified).
why_it_might_be_wrong: Flame color and flicker texture may carry enough signal that models survive unclipped renditions with modest degradation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Apply inverse-clipping simulation (compressing highlights) to existing fire images and measure one model's degradation within hours.

one_line_idea: When intensity and shape cues conflict in medical images, models may follow intensity even where shape says otherwise; the conflict point is measurable.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Lesion segmentation can rely on intensity contrast or on shape context; these usually agree in training data, hiding which cue models actually use. Constructed cue-conflict stimuli can reveal the hierarchy, which matters because pathology often presents with atypical intensity.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On cue-conflict phantoms (lesion-shaped regions with inverted or nulled contrast, and lesion-intensity regions with implausible shapes), models overwhelmingly follow intensity, and the intensity dominance measured on phantoms predicts real-world failure on atypical-presentation cases such as isointense lesions.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The phantom-measured intensity-dominance index will correlate across models with error on curated atypical-intensity clinical cases; no correlation falsifies the diagnostic value of the conflict test.
why_important: Isointense and atypically presenting lesions are precisely the ones humans also miss; knowing that models are pure intensity followers would quantify a shared blind spot and motivate shape-pathway supervision.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Cue-conflict methodology is established in texture-shape classification work; a medical dense-prediction version with clinical validation linkage may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate cue-conflict stimuli by editing real scans (contrast manipulation within anatomically plausible masks), measure per-model cue-following rates, and correlate with performance on a held-out atypical-presentation case set.
main_risk: Edited scans risk leaving editing artifacts that models detect, contaminating the conflict measurement.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Deep segmenters are assumed to integrate shape and context significantly, exceeding classic intensity thresholding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern models with large receptive fields may genuinely use shape context, showing mixed cue-following that defeats the simple dominance narrative.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Create ten contrast-nulled lesion phantoms and check whether two models still find the lesions in a day.

one_line_idea: Smoke may be predicted wherever fire context appears: pasting fire-adjacent context into clean scenes could conjure phantom smoke masks.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Training scenes for smoke overwhelmingly contain co-occurring context (flames, forests, chimneys, emergency lighting); models may segment smoke partly from this context rather than from smoke evidence, producing hallucinated masks in smoke-free but fire-adjacent scenes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Compositing fire-context elements into verified smoke-free scenes induces smoke predictions in regions with no smoke-like appearance, with the induced area growing with context strength, demonstrating a quantifiable context-hallucination pathway distinct from appearance confusion.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Context-injection composites will produce significant phantom smoke area across models, spatially disconnected from injected elements; near-zero phantom area falsifies the context-hallucination claim.
why_important: False alarms in fire monitoring have real costs (suppression dispatch, alarm fatigue); a context pathway would explain false alarms that appearance-based analysis cannot, and would indict co-occurrence statistics in training data.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Context reliance is studied for object recognition; measuring context-induced dense hallucination for safety classes may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a composite test set injecting graded fire context into smoke-free scenes, run several smoke segmenters, and measure phantom mask area versus context dose with compositing-artifact controls.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts may themselves trigger predictions; artifact-only control composites are essential.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] False positives are attributed to smoke-like appearance (fog, steam), not to semantic context priming.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense predictors may be more locally grounded than feared, with context influencing confidence but not creating masks from nothing.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Paste flame crops into ten clean landscape images and check two models for phantom smoke in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Video-compression artifacts may be a learned smoke cue: recompression could move masks more than scene changes do.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Much smoke and fire footage originates from surveillance systems and online video with strong lossy compression, and codecs treat diffuse moving textures distinctively. [HYPOTHESIS] Models may have learned codec signatures (blocking, mosquito noise around soft gradients) as smoke evidence, which would make predictions bitrate-dependent in deployment.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Predicted smoke masks change substantially under recompression sweeps (varying codec and bitrate on identical content), with the direction of change consistent with codec-artifact reliance, and models trained on high-compression sources show the largest sensitivity.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Mask instability across recompression will exceed a tight threshold and correlate with training-source compression statistics; bitrate-invariant masks falsify the codec-cue claim.
why_important: Deployment cameras differ wildly in encoding; codec-dependent perception would produce unexplained site-to-site performance swings and is invisible to standard benchmark practice, which fixes the encoding.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Compression robustness is studied generically; identifying codec artifacts as a positive learned cue for a specific safety class may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Recompress a fixed evaluation set across codecs and bitrates, measure per-model mask drift, and compare drift against content-change baselines.
main_risk: Bitrate changes also remove genuine fine smoke texture; disentangling artifact-cue loss from evidence loss needs synthetic smoke with known ground truth.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Compression is treated as benign nuisance noise handled by augmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Standard augmentation pipelines may already include compression, having inoculated models against codec dependence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Recompress ten test videos at three bitrates and measure one model's mask drift the same day.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: codec-artifact-as-positive-cue is the shortcut-reliance direction; A-038 covers the fragility direction. Related, not duplicate.

one_line_idea: Texture-shape bias may be amplified at segmentation boundaries: per-pixel stylization tests could show boundary decisions are texture-driven where shape should rule.
problem: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK - general] Texture bias in classification networks is established. [HYPOTHESIS] For dense prediction, the interesting question is spatial: whether texture reliance intensifies near boundaries, exactly where hard domains (infiltrative margins, wispy smoke) offer no reliable texture, which would explain concentrated boundary failure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Stylization interventions (texture replacement with shape preserved) perturb predictions disproportionately within a narrow band around boundaries relative to interiors, and this boundary texture-dependence is largest in the hard domains of this territory, revealing a spatially structured shortcut invisible to image-level bias measures.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Prediction-change maps under stylization will concentrate in boundary bands with an interior-to-boundary ratio far below one; spatially uniform perturbation sensitivity falsifies the boundary-amplification claim.
why_important: It localizes the texture-bias problem to where hard domains actually fail, and implies boundary-specific remedies (shape-biased boundary decoding) rather than global stylization augmentation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Texture-bias literature reports image-level effects; a per-pixel spatial decomposition of cue reliance in dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply structure-preserving stylization to evaluation images, compute per-pixel prediction change, stratify by distance to ground-truth boundary, and compare across domains and models.
main_risk: Stylization inevitably alters some shape-adjacent cues (local contrast), requiring multiple stylization operators to triangulate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Texture bias is an image-level property, treated with global augmentation; spatial structure of the bias is not part of the discussion.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary regions might show high sensitivity to any perturbation simply because decisions there sit near the margin, requiring margin-controlled analysis to avoid triviality.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Stylize five images, plot the prediction-change-versus-boundary-distance curve for one model in a day.

judge_C_adversary.reason: Texture-vs-shape cue conflict for segmentation; boundary-band localization is an analysis choice, not a new hypothesis.

one_line_idea: Single-frame smoke benchmarks may leak motion information through blur signatures, inflating reported single-image capability.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Frames extracted from video retain motion blur, and moving smoke produces characteristic directional blur patterns. [HYPOTHESIS] Purportedly single-image smoke segmentation may exploit these temporal residues, overstating what is achievable from genuinely static observation and misleading sensor-design conclusions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models evaluated on deblurred or fast-shutter versions of benchmark frames lose a substantial share of their smoke segmentation performance, revealing that part of the claimed single-frame capability is hidden temporal information rather than static appearance understanding.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Performance on blur-removed frames will drop significantly more for smoke than for static-object classes in the same frames; equal drops falsify the motion-leakage claim.
why_important: System designers choose between single-frame and temporal architectures based on benchmark evidence; leakage-corrupted evidence leads to under-provisioned temporal modeling in deployed safety systems.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Benchmark leakage studies focus on duplicates and label leakage; motion-blur as an information side channel in single-frame evaluation may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct paired evaluations with original frames and deblurred counterparts (algorithmic deblurring validated on static content), compare smoke-class degradation against static-class degradation across models.
main_risk: Deblurring introduces its own artifacts; a static-class control and multiple deblurring methods are needed to attribute the drop correctly.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Single-frame evaluation is assumed to measure static-appearance understanding by construction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At typical surveillance shutter speeds smoke motion blur may be negligible, making the side channel empty.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare one model on ten original versus deblurred frames and check the smoke-specific drop within a day.

one_line_idea: Smoke versus steam versus fog: current models may be undifferentiated haze detectors, and a confusability audit would expose the semantic emptiness.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Steam, fog, dust, and smoke are optically similar participating media with different safety semantics. [HYPOTHESIS] Models labeled as smoke detectors may be detecting generic haze, with class identity supplied by dataset context rather than perception, which would make their semantic label scientifically and practically misleading.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On a balanced cross-media test set, smoke segmenters will fire near-equally on steam, fog, and dust once scene context is neutralized, and their discrimination ability will collapse toward chance under context randomization, showing the smoke label reflects dataset co-occurrence, not media identification.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Context-neutralized discrimination between smoke and other media will be near chance for current models; strong above-chance discrimination falsifies the haze-detector claim.
why_important: The smoke-versus-steam distinction is the difference between an alarm and a false alarm in industrial settings; knowing whether the distinction is perceptual or contextual determines what data must be collected next.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Hard-negative evaluation exists piecemeal; a systematic cross-media confusability audit with context neutralization may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble media-balanced clips with verified physical identity (industrial steam vents, fog banks, controlled smoke), neutralize context via cropping and background randomization, and measure per-media response rates of several models.
main_risk: Ground-truth media identity requires provenance verification, which limits scalable data collection.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Published per-class scores are taken to mean models distinguish these media perceptually.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Subtle cues (steam dissipation profile, smoke coloration from combustion products) may actually be learned, giving genuine discrimination even without context.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run one smoke model on twenty steam and fog clips with tight crops and count false fires in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Pixelwise calibration can be perfect while extent estimates are wildly miscalibrated, because dense errors are spatially correlated; extent-level calibration is the missing target.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Segmentation errors are spatially correlated (whole regions are missed together), while calibration is almost always measured pixelwise. [HYPOTHESIS] This mismatch may allow models to pass pixel-level calibration audits while producing region-area estimates whose confidence intervals are meaningless, which is what downstream users actually consume.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models with near-perfect pixelwise expected calibration exhibit severe miscalibration of derived quantities (total area, structure count, extent percentile), with realized coverage of area confidence intervals far below nominal, because correlated errors violate the independence implicitly assumed when aggregating pixel probabilities.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] On any hard-domain dataset, area confidence intervals derived from pixelwise-calibrated probabilities will show realized coverage dramatically below nominal; near-nominal coverage falsifies the correlated-error account.
why_important: Clinical volume estimates and fire-extent reports rely on aggregated dense outputs; a systematic gap between pixel and aggregate calibration is a silent safety defect that current audit practice cannot detect.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Pixel calibration and structure-level uncertainty are both studied, but a direct demonstration that one systematically fails to imply the other, with a proposed extent-calibration metric, may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Calibrate a model pixelwise via temperature scaling, derive area confidence intervals under independence, and measure realized coverage against ground truth areas across test cases.
main_risk: The result may be seen as mathematically expected; the contribution must be the magnitude measurement and the corrected aggregation method.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] A pixelwise-calibrated segmentation model is considered a calibrated model.

one_line_idea: Partial coverage and uncertainty are confounded in soft masks: a probability of one half can mean half-covered or fully-unknown, and the two need different downstream actions.

one_line_idea: Copy-paste augmentation is physically invalid for participating media: pasted smoke without recomputed attenuation may teach models compositing artifacts as the cue.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Smoke models trained with naive copy-paste augmentation respond more strongly to compositing artifacts than to physical smoke cues (verified by artifact-only probes), and physically corrected compositing (attenuation-aware blending) removes this artifact reliance while preserving augmentation benefits, isolating a data-pipeline cause of real-world brittleness.
