The fraction of current model error that lies within the plausible-rater set on hard domains has not been measured, yet it determines how much of the reported gap is real (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under distribution-matching evaluation (a prediction is correct where it falls within the empirical rater distribution), a substantial fraction of state-of-the-art model error on ambiguous structures disappears, and model rankings change, revealing that current one-mask evaluation systematically misrepresents both absolute and relative performance in this territory.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-scoring several models on multi-rater data will reclassify a large share of ambiguous-region errors as within-distribution and produce ranking shifts; negligible reclassification falsifies the misrepresentation claim.
why_important: If a big share of measured error is disagreement with one arbitrary rater rather than mistake, the field's progress narrative and its method rankings on hard domains both need revision, and evaluation infrastructure should move to distribution-based scoring.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Multi-rater evaluation metrics exist in the probabilistic segmentation literature; a systematic error-reclassification audit of standard models and rankings across this territory may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-rater datasets across the territory, evaluate a model zoo under single-reference and distribution-matching protocols, quantify reclassified error share, and compare rankings.
main_risk: With few raters the empirical distribution is undersampled, inflating the within-distribution region and over-crediting models.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Deviation from the reference mask is error, full stop; evaluation practice encodes this belief everywhere.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may err in directions no rater ever takes (implausible shapes), leaving reclassification shares small and the standard evaluation vindicated.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-score one model on one multi-rater structure set under both protocols in a day and measure the reclassified share.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Co-primary of dg04 (segmentation instantiation of distribution-matching evaluation); pairs with C-066 for the classification/superhuman side.

one_line_idea: Fixed-bin expected calibration error systematically misranks vision foundation models compared to debiased or binning-free calibration estimators.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Expected calibration error with a fixed number of equal-width confidence bins is the dominant reported calibration metric, and it is known in the statistics literature that binned estimators are biased.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For modern high-accuracy vision foundation models whose confidence distributions are heavily skewed toward 1.0, fixed-bin ECE bias is large enough to change model rankings relative to debiased or kernel-based estimators.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Ranking a pool of public vision models by fixed-bin ECE versus a debiased estimator on the same predictions will produce at least some pairwise rank inversions, concentrated among high-accuracy models.
why_important: If the standard metric misranks models, published calibration comparisons and papers claiming calibration improvements may be reporting estimator artifacts.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Estimator bias is documented in the calibration literature, but a focused audit showing rank inversions specifically among current large vision models may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect logits from a set of public vision models on one test set, compute fixed-bin ECE and two alternative estimators, and quantify rank agreement plus bootstrap uncertainty on each estimate.
main_risk: Rank inversions may exist but fall within bootstrap noise, making the contrarian claim technically true but practically inconsequential.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners treat 15-bin ECE as an adequate default and assume estimator choice does not change qualitative conclusions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The confidence distributions of modern models are far more extreme than those of the older models on which binning conventions were established.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Reuse cached logits from any two models, compute three calibration estimators, and check for a rank flip; this requires no new model inference.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: In-distribution calibration of vision foundation models carries near-zero information about their calibration under distribution shift.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Calibration is usually measured on the in-distribution test split, and models are then deployed under shift where the measurement may not transfer.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across a pool of vision foundation models, the correlation between in-distribution calibration error and calibration error on shifted variants of the same task is weak or absent once accuracy is controlled for.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A scatter of in-distribution versus shifted calibration error across many public checkpoints will show low partial correlation after conditioning on accuracy, and model selection by in-distribution calibration will fail to select the best-calibrated model under shift.
why_important: Practitioners select and temperature-tune models using in-distribution calibration; if that transfers poorly, deployed confidence estimates are systematically misleading exactly when they matter most.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prior work has observed calibration degradation under shift, but framing it as a model-selection failure with an accuracy-controlled correlation analysis across modern foundation models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 15 or more public checkpoints on one standard test set and two or more shifted counterparts, compute calibration on each, and measure rank correlation of calibration across distributions with accuracy partialled out.
main_risk: Available shifted test sets may share construction artifacts, so the measured transfer failure could reflect benchmark idiosyncrasy rather than a general law.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A model that is well calibrated in distribution is assumed to be a comparatively safer choice under shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Calibration under shift may be governed by how the confidence distribution deforms with input corruption, which is unrelated to the in-distribution calibration offset that temperature scaling fixes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Use publicly released prediction files where available for a handful of models on a standard set and one shifted set, and compute the cross-distribution calibration rank correlation without running any inference.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Full fine-tuning of vision foundation models improves in-distribution accuracy while systematically destroying calibration transferability relative to linear probing.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Fine-tuning versus linear probing is usually compared on accuracy, with calibration under subsequent shift rarely part of the comparison.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Linear probes on frozen foundation features retain better-calibrated and more shift-stable confidence than full fine-tuning of the same backbone, even when full fine-tuning wins on accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across several downstream tasks, the fine-tuned models will show larger calibration degradation from in-distribution to shifted evaluation than their linear-probe counterparts trained on identical data.
why_important: Teams default to full fine-tuning for accuracy; if it silently trades away confidence reliability, risk-sensitive applications should prefer probes or partial tuning.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The accuracy-robustness effects of fine-tuning have been studied, but a dedicated calibration-transfer comparison between probing and full tuning at foundation scale may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one backbone and three downstream datasets with shifted variants, train a linear probe and a full fine-tune per dataset, then compare calibration error in and out of distribution.
main_risk: The result may depend heavily on fine-tuning hyperparameters such as learning rate and epochs, making the claim about a recipe rather than about fine-tuning per se.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Full fine-tuning is assumed to dominate linear probing whenever enough downstream data exists.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuning reshapes the feature space toward the downstream label set and may discard the density information in pretrained features that supports honest uncertainty.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, one dataset with an existing shifted variant, one probe and one fine-tune, four calibration numbers; a single-GPU day.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept but verify prior art: fine-tuning-distorts-features / calibration literature is adjacent; the calibration-transferability framing is the retained content.

one_line_idea: Verbalized confidence from multimodal vision-language models is systematically less reliable than their own token-level log-probabilities on visual questions, contradicting the intuition that self-reports add information.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multimodal assistants are often asked to state their confidence in words, and such verbalized scores are increasingly used as the uncertainty interface in applications.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On visual question answering, verbalized confidence is a coarse social artifact that clusters at a few round values and carries less error-predictive information than the answer token log-probability of the same model.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For the same model and question set, error-detection metrics computed from verbalized confidence will be worse than those computed from answer token log-probabilities, and the verbalized distribution will show heavy heaping on round numbers.
why_important: Product designs that surface verbalized confidence to users may be surfacing the weaker of two available uncertainty signals.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Verbalized calibration has been studied for text-only models, but a controlled comparison against internal log-probabilities specifically on visual grounding tasks may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run one open-weight multimodal model on a visual question set, record both verbalized confidence and token log-probabilities, and compare their error-prediction quality on the same items.
main_risk: Prompt wording for eliciting verbalized confidence is itself a free parameter, so the comparison must sweep elicitation prompts to be fair.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Many practitioners assume that asking the model for its confidence extracts calibrated self-knowledge unavailable in raw logits.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Verbalized numbers are generated by the same next-token machinery, filtered through instruction-tuning biases that reward confident-sounding answers.
fastest_falsification_experiment: A few hundred visual questions on one open-weight model with both signals logged; a single evening of inference.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept but verify prior art: verbalized-confidence literature is active in LLMs; vision-specific claim retained.

one_line_idea: Aggregate calibration hides severe tail-class miscalibration: vision foundation models that look calibrated on average are strongly overconfident exactly on rare classes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Calibration is almost always reported as a single dataset-level number, while class frequency distributions in benchmarks are heavily imbalanced.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dataset-level calibration is dominated by head classes, and per-class calibration error grows sharply with class rarity, so a single number certifies nothing about tail behavior.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stratifying calibration by class frequency for public checkpoints will show a monotone-ish degradation toward the tail, with tail-class calibration error several times the aggregate value.
why_important: Rare classes are often the operationally critical ones, and overconfidence there is precisely the failure mode aggregate metrics are supposed to guard against.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Class-wise calibration has been discussed for small models and long-tail literature, but an audit establishing the aggregate-versus-tail gap for modern foundation models may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class calibration curves on one large labeled test set for several checkpoints, bin classes by frequency, and compare aggregate versus tail-bin calibration error.
main_risk: Per-class calibration estimates on rare classes are noisy, so the analysis needs hierarchical pooling or frequency-bin aggregation to be credible.
community_default_belief: [KNOWN FACT] The standard reporting convention treats one dataset-level calibration number as an adequate summary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: An average over a power-law class distribution mathematically cannot constrain the behavior on classes contributing negligible mass to the average.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One checkpoint, one test set, calibration computed on the top decile versus bottom decile of class frequency; an hour with cached predictions.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: tail-class calibration concealment; template-similar to C-044 (accuracy version) but the measured quantity differs; both retained with the similarity noted.

one_line_idea: Post-hoc calibration methods evaluated on held-out splits of the same distribution overstate their value because the fitted correction does not transfer across datasets.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Temperature scaling and similar corrections are standardly fitted and evaluated on splits of the same dataset, and reported as making models calibrated.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Corrections fitted on one dataset transfer poorly to other datasets and to shifted inputs, sometimes making calibration worse than the uncorrected model, so the standard protocol measures interpolation rather than calibration repair.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A transfer matrix of corrections fitted on dataset A and evaluated on dataset B across several datasets will show frequent negative transfer, concentrated where confidence distributions differ.
why_important: The belief that a cheap post-hoc step makes any model calibrated underwrites a lot of deployment practice; if the step is distribution-bound, the guarantee is illusory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Failure of temperature transfer under shift has been noted, but a systematic cross-dataset transfer matrix at foundation scale with negative-transfer accounting may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit temperature and vector scaling per source dataset for several checkpoints, evaluate all corrections on all target datasets, and count negative-transfer cells.
main_risk: Datasets vary in label granularity and head structure, so cross-dataset evaluation must be restricted to comparable prediction setups to be meaningful.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Temperature scaling is treated as a solved-problem fix that generalizes wherever the model is used.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A single scalar correction can only shift the confidence distribution globally, while the miscalibration structure is input-dependent and shifts with the data.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One checkpoint, temperatures fitted on two datasets, cross-evaluated; four numbers from cached logits.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: A measurable share of apparent overconfidence in vision foundation models is actually test-label error, and models are better calibrated with respect to corrected labels.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark test labels contain errors, and calibration is computed against those labels as if they were ground truth.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] High-confidence disagreements between strong models and test labels are enriched for label errors, so measured overconfidence partially reflects annotation noise rather than model miscalibration.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Human re-adjudication of high-confidence model-label disagreements will find a substantial label-error rate, and recomputing calibration with adjudicated labels will reduce measured overconfidence for the strongest models more than for weaker ones.
why_important: If the metric penalizes correctness, calibration research is partly optimizing models toward reproducing annotation mistakes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label-error effects on accuracy rankings are documented, but a quantitative decomposition of calibration error into label-noise and model components may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample high-confidence disagreements for a few checkpoints on one benchmark, re-adjudicate with multiple annotators, and recompute calibration curves under corrected labels.
main_risk: Adjudication itself is noisy and potentially biased toward plausible-looking model answers, requiring blinded protocols.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Measured overconfidence is interpreted as a defect of the model rather than of the labels.
why_it_might_be_wrong: As models exceed annotator accuracy, the disagreement set flips from being mostly model errors to being substantially label errors, and the calibration metric does not know this.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Manually inspect 100 highest-confidence disagreements of one strong checkpoint on one benchmark and count evident label errors; one day of annotation.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Calibration evaluation for detection and segmentation is ill-defined as currently practiced because the confidence scores are ranking scores, not probabilities of any explicit event.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detector confidence scores are consumed by threshold-based matching and non-maximum suppression, yet calibration analyses often treat them as probabilities of correct detection.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because the event a detection score should predict depends on matching criteria, thresholds, and duplicate suppression, published detector calibration numbers are protocol artifacts that change qualitatively under alternative but equally defensible event definitions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Recomputing detector calibration under several defensible event definitions will change which detector counts as best calibrated on the same predictions.
why_important: Downstream systems consume detector scores as if they were probabilities; without a fixed event semantics, any calibration claim is unfalsifiable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Detection calibration papers exist, but a formal argument plus empirical demonstration that the metric is underdetermined by the prediction format may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take public detection outputs from a few models, define three event semantics for score correctness, compute calibration under each, and test ranking stability.
main_risk: The critique could be dismissed as pedantic unless a downstream decision cost difference is demonstrated between semantics.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detector confidence is assumed to be an approximate probability whose calibration can be measured like a classifier probability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The score is trained and post-processed for average-precision ranking, an objective indifferent to any probabilistic semantics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One detector output file, two event definitions, two calibration curves; an afternoon with no GPU.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Ensembles of vision foundation models improve calibration mostly by uniformly shrinking confidence rather than by improving the ranking of which inputs are risky.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Deep ensembles are the standard strong baseline for calibrated uncertainty, and their calibration gains are usually reported as a single error reduction.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Decomposing ensemble calibration gains into a global confidence-shift component and an input-ranking component will show the shift component dominates, meaning a temperature-scaled single model captures most of the benefit.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] After optimal temperature scaling of the single best member, the residual calibration and selective-prediction advantage of the ensemble will be small on in-distribution data, with a modest remainder under shift.
why_important: Ensembles multiply inference cost; if their uncertainty benefit is mostly a scalar shift, the cost is unjustified for many deployments.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Comparisons of ensembles versus temperature scaling exist, but a clean shift-versus-ranking decomposition on modern foundation checkpoints may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build an ensemble from public checkpoints, compare its risk-coverage and calibration curves against the temperature-scaled best member in and out of distribution.
main_risk: Ensemble members built from independently pretrained foundation models may be unusually diverse, which would strengthen the ranking component and refute the claim.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Ensembles are believed to provide qualitatively better uncertainty, not just rescaled confidence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Members trained on similar web-scale data may make correlated errors, leaving averaging with little ranking information to add.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three public checkpoints, cached logits on one test set plus one shifted set, ensemble versus tempered single-model curves; no training required.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: The epistemic-aleatoric uncertainty decomposition reported for vision models is not identifiable in practice: interventions designed to change one component move both estimates.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many uncertainty methods report separate epistemic and aleatoric components, and papers interpret them as capturing model ignorance versus data noise.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under controlled interventions, such as adding label noise to change aleatoric uncertainty or shrinking training data to change epistemic uncertainty, popular estimators will show strong cross-contamination, invalidating the interpretation of the components.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A two-factor intervention grid of label-noise level versus training-set size will show that both reported components respond substantially to both factors for common estimators.
why_important: Downstream decisions such as when to collect more data versus when to accept irreducible error rely on the decomposition meaning what it claims.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Identifiability critiques exist in the theory literature, but a systematic interventional audit on vision backbones at realistic scale may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train small-to-medium vision models across a grid of dataset sizes and injected label-noise rates, compute component estimates from two or three popular methods, and quantify cross-responsiveness.
main_risk: The result at small scale may not represent foundation-scale behavior, requiring at least one large-backbone replication via fine-tuning.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The two reported components are assumed to be approximately separable measurements of distinct quantities.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The decomposition is derived under Bayesian assumptions that deep approximations do not satisfy, so the components are functions of the approximation quality rather than of the underlying quantities.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One small backbone, a 3-by-3 grid of noise and data size, one estimator; a weekend of GPU time.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Marginal coverage claims of conformal prediction on vision benchmarks conceal severe conditional coverage failures under realistic covariate shift.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Conformal prediction guarantees marginal coverage under exchangeability, and vision papers report empirical coverage on iid splits as validation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On realistic shifted or subgroup-structured vision data, marginal coverage remains superficially acceptable while coverage conditional on subgroups or shift severity collapses, making the reported guarantee operationally misleading.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating conformal classifiers stratified by corruption severity, subpopulation, or capture condition will show large coverage deficits in some strata alongside near-nominal marginal coverage.
why_important: Conformal methods are being promoted as deployment-grade uncertainty for vision; users reading a marginal guarantee will assume per-case reliability it does not provide.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Conditional-coverage limitations are known theoretically, but a broad empirical audit across vision foundation models and realistic strata may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Calibrate standard conformal wrappers on a clean split for several checkpoints, evaluate stratified coverage across shifted variants and metadata subgroups, and report worst-stratum coverage.
main_risk: Choice of strata is a researcher degree of freedom; pre-registering strata is needed for the audit to be convincing.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A validated marginal coverage number is taken as evidence the uncertainty sets are trustworthy in use.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Exchangeability is exactly the assumption deployment violates, and marginal averaging is exactly the mechanism that hides where it breaks.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One checkpoint, one conformal wrapper, coverage stratified by available metadata on one shifted set; a few hours from cached logits.

judge_C_adversary.reason: One shifted-conformal study should report conditional coverage and set-size utility together; two symptoms, one evaluation.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Co-primary of dg28: absorbs C-022 (set-size utility corollary); prior-art risk on conditional-coverage impossibility noted.

one_line_idea: Standard out-of-distribution detection benchmarks are largely solvable by trivial low-level statistics, so reported method rankings measure benchmark artifacts.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Out-of-distribution detection methods are compared on benchmark pairs of in-distribution and outlier datasets that often differ in acquisition pipeline, resolution, and compression history.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Simple input-level statistics such as compressed file size, color histogram distance, or embedding norm achieve detection performance close to sophisticated methods on standard pairs, implying the pairs mostly measure pipeline mismatch.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A basket of trivial detectors will reach a large fraction of the reported performance of leading methods on legacy benchmark pairs, but the gap will widen substantially on pipeline-matched near-distribution pairs.
why_important: If leaderboards are saturated by artifacts, method development is being steered toward exploiting acquisition signatures rather than semantic novelty detection.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual artifact critiques have appeared over the years, but a comprehensive trivial-baseline audit against current foundation-model-era methods may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement five trivial detectors, run them on several standard benchmark pairs plus one carefully pipeline-matched pair, and compare against published-method reproductions run locally.
main_risk: Constructing genuinely pipeline-matched pairs is hard, and errors there would undermine the contrast the audit depends on.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark gains in out-of-distribution detection are read as progress in modeling semantic novelty.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dataset pairs assembled from different sources differ in dozens of shallow statistics, and any detector can win by keying on them.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compressed-size and embedding-norm detectors on two standard pairs, compared to locally reproduced standard baselines; one day, minimal GPU.

judge_C_adversary.reason: Restates the long-standing critique that OOD benchmarks fall to trivial low-level statistics; hedged in tone but adds no new mechanism or protocol beyond re-running known baselines. Unverified prior-art risk: very high.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept but verify prior art: OOD-benchmark triviality critiques exist; the systematic low-level-statistics audit is the retained content.

one_line_idea: Uncertainty-method rankings established on small networks and datasets invert at foundation scale, so the field's canonical conclusions may not transfer to the models people actually deploy.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Much of the comparative uncertainty literature was established on small benchmarks and architectures because rigorous Bayesian baselines are expensive.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Relative performance of uncertainty methods is scale-dependent: methods that win at small scale, such as sampling-based approaches, lose to deterministic feature-based approaches once representations come from large pretrained backbones.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A fixed battery of uncertainty methods evaluated across a scale ladder from small supervised models to large pretrained backbones will show statistically significant rank inversions between the smallest and largest rungs.
why_important: Practitioners inherit method recommendations from small-scale studies; if rankings invert, those recommendations actively misguide deployment choices.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scale-dependence of accuracy phenomena is well studied, but a controlled scale-ladder study of uncertainty method rankings may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate four or five uncertainty methods at three scale rungs on matched tasks, holding evaluation protocol fixed, and test ranking stability across rungs.
main_risk: Scale is confounded with pretraining data and objective; the ladder must vary one factor at a time where possible.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Uncertainty method quality is treated as roughly architecture- and scale-independent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information available to uncertainty methods changes qualitatively when representations are learned from web-scale data rather than the task data alone.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two rungs, three methods, one task family; check for a single robust inversion in a few GPU-days.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Primary keep of dg05 umbrella: absorbs C-005 (kNN), C-014 (MC dropout null), C-017 (embedding norm) as arms of one scale-dependence study.

one_line_idea: Test-time-augmentation-based uncertainty mostly measures a model's augmentation sensitivity, not its predictive uncertainty, and the two decouple under simple interventions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Variance of predictions across test-time augmentations is a popular uncertainty proxy because it needs no training changes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Augmentation variance is governed by how the training recipe handled those augmentations, so models trained with heavy augmentation look spuriously certain, and the proxy fails to track error probability across recipes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing checkpoints that differ mainly in augmentation recipe will show large differences in augmentation-variance uncertainty at matched error rates, and within any single model the proxy will underperform simple logit-based signals for error detection.
why_important: The proxy is used in medical and safety pipelines where a recipe-driven artifact masquerading as uncertainty is dangerous.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Test-time augmentation is well studied for accuracy, but a recipe-controlled critique of its uncertainty interpretation may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take public checkpoints with documented light versus heavy augmentation recipes, compute augmentation-variance uncertainty and error-detection quality, and compare at matched accuracy.
main_risk: Public checkpoints rarely isolate augmentation as the only recipe difference, so a small controlled training run may be needed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Instability under augmentation is assumed to indicate the model is unsure about the input.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Invariance is a trained property, so its absence indicates a recipe gap rather than input difficulty.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two public checkpoints with different augmentation recipes, one test set, compare augmentation-variance versus logit-gap error detection in a day.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: For multimodal models, answer instability across paraphrased visual prompts predicts errors better than the model's own internal confidence signals.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Uncertainty for multimodal assistants is usually derived from token log-probabilities of a single prompt, while the same question can be asked many ways.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Semantic disagreement of answers across paraphrases is a stronger and more shift-robust error predictor than single-prompt log-probability, because it probes representation stability rather than decoder fluency.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On visual question sets, paraphrase-disagreement scores will dominate single-prompt log-probability on error-detection metrics, with the advantage growing on harder or shifted images.
why_important: It gives a black-box uncertainty method usable on closed models where logits are unavailable, and challenges the assumption that internal signals are strictly more informative.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Consistency-based uncertainty exists for text models, but a systematic comparison against internal signals for visual question answering may be thin.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate several paraphrases per question, run one open multimodal model, score semantic agreement, and compare error-detection quality against token log-probabilities on the same items.
main_risk: Paraphrase generation may leak difficulty information or change question semantics, requiring careful paraphrase validation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Internal logits are assumed to upper-bound the information available from black-box sampling behavior.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decoder confidence reflects language fluency and answer-format priors, while paraphrase consistency directly stresses the visual grounding that determines correctness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three paraphrases for a few hundred questions on one open model; compare the two error-detection curves in one evening.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Error-detection AUROC as the standard uncertainty metric structurally favors accurate models, so uncertainty leaderboards partly re-measure accuracy.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Uncertainty quality is commonly summarized by how well confidence separates correct from incorrect predictions, compared across models with different accuracies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because the composition of the error set changes with accuracy, cross-model comparisons of error-detection metrics confound uncertainty quality with accuracy, and accuracy-controlled evaluations will rerank methods and models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating uncertainty on matched-difficulty item subsets or via accuracy-stratified metrics will change model orderings relative to raw error-detection scores in a reproducible way.
why_important: The field may be crediting models with better uncertainty when they simply make fewer, harder errors, distorting method development.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The confounding is occasionally acknowledged in passing, but a formal analysis with a corrected metric and a demonstration of reranking at foundation scale may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct accuracy-matched evaluation subsets across checkpoints of different strengths and compare raw versus matched uncertainty rankings.
main_risk: Matching item difficulty across models is itself model-dependent, requiring an external difficulty estimate to avoid circularity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Error-detection metrics are treated as accuracy-independent measures of uncertainty quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A metric defined over a model-dependent partition of items cannot be compared across models whose partitions differ systematically.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Simulate predictions with controlled accuracy and identical uncertainty mechanisms, show the metric moves with accuracy alone; hours on a laptop.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Primary keep of dg26: absorbs C-041 (FPR-at-TPR reordering).

one_line_idea: Contamination of vision benchmarks by web-scale pretraining is systematically underestimated because deduplication tools detect pixel duplicates but not semantic duplicates of the same scene.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Foundation-model training sets are scraped from the web where benchmark images circulate in edited, cropped, re-encoded, and re-photographed forms, while contamination audits typically rely on perceptual-hash or embedding near-duplicate detection.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial contamination tail consists of same-scene variants that evade standard near-duplicate thresholds yet still leak test-specific information, so published contamination rates are lower bounds with material undercounting.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A retrieval protocol tuned for same-scene matching, followed by human verification, will surface leaked variants for benchmark images at a rate meaningfully above what perceptual-hash audits report on the same corpus.
why_important: Zero-shot and few-shot claims for foundation models rest on the assumption that test content is unseen; undercounted leakage inflates the field's headline results.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Contamination auditing exists, but a same-scene leakage estimator with human-verified precision, applied to open pretraining corpora, may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one benchmark and one open pretraining corpus, run scene-level retrieval with geometric verification, human-verify a sample of matches missed by standard dedup, and extrapolate an undercount rate.
main_risk: Same-scene matching without ground truth risks false positives; human verification of a statistically sufficient sample is labor-intensive.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Passing a perceptual-hash dedup audit is treated as demonstrating a benchmark is effectively uncontaminated.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Information leakage operates at the level of scene content and annotation conventions, not pixel identity, and dedup tools only see the latter.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Manually image-search 50 benchmark test images against an open corpus index and count human-confirmed same-scene variants missed by hash dedup; two days of analyst time.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Primary keep of dg20: absorbs C-026 (generative derivatives) and C-093 (template reuse) as contamination channels.

one_line_idea: Zero-shot performance of vision foundation models is mostly seen-shot: accuracy stratified by similarity to pretraining data reveals the claimed generalization is concentrated where near-training content exists.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Zero-shot evaluation treats all test items equally, while pretraining corpora cover web content unevenly, and similarity of each test item to pretraining data is rarely reported.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-item zero-shot accuracy is strongly increasing in pretraining-similarity, and the low-similarity stratum shows dramatically weaker performance, meaning aggregate zero-shot numbers substantially overstate generalization to genuinely novel content.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stratifying a standard zero-shot benchmark by retrieval-based similarity to an open pretraining corpus will show a steep accuracy gradient, with the bottom stratum far below the aggregate number for the same model.
why_important: The zero-shot framing drives adoption decisions and scientific claims about emergent generalization; a similarity gradient reframes those claims as retrieval coverage.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Similarity-stratified analysis has appeared in isolated studies, but making it a standard reporting axis with open tooling across models and benchmarks may be unclaimed territory.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Index one open pretraining corpus, compute per-test-item max-similarity for one benchmark, stratify accuracy for several checkpoints, and report gradient slopes.
main_risk: Similarity computed in the model's own embedding space is circular; an independent similarity measure or multiple measures are needed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Aggregate zero-shot accuracy is read as evidence of broad generalization beyond training data coverage.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web-scale corpora plausibly contain close relatives of most benchmark content, so the aggregate is dominated by the high-similarity stratum by construction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one benchmark, similarity from an off-the-shelf retrieval index, quartile-stratified accuracy; a day once the index exists.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Primary keep of dg02: A-070 (SAM/SA-1B) merged in as the segmentation case study; overlap-stratified evaluation is the shared design.

one_line_idea: Annotation error rates in flagship vision test sets exceed the score gaps separating leading foundation models, so leaderboard order among top models is not measurable with current labels.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Label errors in widely used test sets are documented to exist, while top-model score gaps have shrunk as models improve.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For the current top cohort on mature benchmarks, plausible label-error configurations change pairwise orderings, meaning the benchmark no longer has the resolving power for its primary use of ranking frontier models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A sensitivity analysis that re-scores leading public checkpoints under adjudicated or perturbed label sets, at error rates consistent with independent re-annotation studies, will flip a nontrivial fraction of top pairwise comparisons.
why_important: Rankings on mature benchmarks still steer publications, releases, and procurement; if the instrument's noise floor exceeds the effects measured, those decisions are arbitrary.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label-error studies and top-gap observations exist separately; an explicit resolving-power analysis framing benchmarks as measurement instruments with noise floors may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take public predictions of five leading checkpoints on one mature benchmark, re-adjudicate a stratified item sample, model label-error uncertainty, and propagate it to ranking confidence.
main_risk: Re-adjudication introduces its own biases, so multiple independent annotator pools and blinding to model outputs are required.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A higher benchmark score, even by a fraction of a point, is treated as evidence one model is better.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A fixed label set with a stable error rate creates a noise floor, and effects below that floor are unfalsifiable claims dressed as measurements.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Bootstrap plus synthetic label-noise injection at documented error rates on cached predictions of three models; one afternoon, no annotation.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Val and test splits of legacy vision benchmarks are non-iid due to photographer, session, and source-page leakage, inflating scores relative to honest disjoint splits.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many benchmark splits were created by randomizing over images rather than over capture sessions, photographers, or source websites.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Same-source images straddling the train-test boundary let models exploit source-specific signatures, and re-splitting by source will measurably reduce scores and change model rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Clustering benchmark images by source metadata or visual-source signatures and re-evaluating with source-disjoint splits will lower absolute scores for all models and shift some pairwise orderings, with larger drops for models fine-tuned on the train split.
why_important: Split leakage is a mundane but compounding score inflator that gets rediscovered per-domain; a general audit would recalibrate expectations across benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Source leakage is documented in specific domains such as medical imaging, but a cross-benchmark audit with a reusable source-clustering tool for mainstream vision test sets may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one benchmark with recoverable source metadata, build source-disjoint splits, fine-tune and evaluate several models on both split types, and compare score distributions.
main_risk: Source metadata is often unavailable, forcing reliance on inferred source clusters whose errors blur the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Random image-level splits are assumed to give unbiased generalization estimates.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Images are not the sampling unit of the underlying data-generating process; sources are, and ignoring the hierarchy is textbook pseudo-replication.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train a source-signature classifier on train-split images and test whether it transfers to test-split images far above chance; a few hours if any source labels exist.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Primary keep of dg03 umbrella (non-iid split leakage): absorbs B-088 (smoke/fire video splits), C-033 (retrieval galleries), C-099 (temporal collection order).

one_line_idea: Synthetic corruption benchmarks poorly predict degradation on real-world image quality problems, so corruption-robustness scores are a misleading proxy for deployment robustness.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Robustness is commonly summarized by accuracy on synthetically corrupted test sets built from a fixed set of algorithmic corruption functions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The correlation between synthetic-corruption robustness and robustness to naturally degraded captures, such as low light, motion blur from real camera shake, and compression from real pipelines, is weak across models once accuracy is controlled.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a paired evaluation of matched scenes captured under real degradation versus synthetically corrupted clean captures, cross-model rank correlation between the two robustness scores will be low, and interventions tuned on synthetic corruptions will show limited transfer.
why_important: Teams optimize augmentations and select models on synthetic suites; if the proxy is weak, deployment robustness engineering is aimed at the wrong target.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Concerns about synthetic corruptions exist, but a paired same-scene real-versus-synthetic degradation dataset enabling a direct proxy-validity measurement may be rare or absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture or assemble a paired set of scenes under controlled real degradations and matched synthetic counterparts, evaluate a pool of checkpoints on both, and measure proxy validity.
main_risk: Building a genuinely paired real-degradation set is the hard part and dominates the cost of the project.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic corruption suites are treated as an adequate stand-in for natural degradation robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Real degradations are physically coupled to scene content and camera behavior in ways fixed algorithmic corruptions do not simulate.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Use an existing small paired-capture dataset or capture 200 paired photos with and without induced real blur, then compare model rankings across real versus synthetic blur in days.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Benchmark aging is real: category semantics and visual distributions drift over time, so accuracy on decade-old test sets overstates accuracy on the same nominal task today.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Flagship vision benchmarks were collected years ago, while the visual world, such as product designs, vehicles, fashion, and interfaces, keeps changing.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For temporally sensitive categories, models score systematically lower on freshly collected same-protocol test items than on the original test sets, and the gap grows with collection-time distance, making benchmark age a quantifiable error term.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A freshly collected replica of a subset of categories using the original collection protocol will show a systematic accuracy drop concentrated in categories whose visual instantiation drifts, and the drop will correlate with independent measures of category drift.
why_important: Reported benchmark accuracy is implicitly used as an estimate of present-day task accuracy; an age-dependent bias term changes how numbers should be read and how benchmarks should be maintained.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Replication studies of benchmarks exist for distribution-shift purposes, but framing and measuring benchmark age as a decaying validity coefficient per category may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Recollect 20 drift-prone and 20 drift-stable categories under the original protocol, evaluate public checkpoints on old versus new items, and estimate the age effect with category-type interaction.
main_risk: Protocol replication is imperfect, and collection differences could masquerade as temporal drift.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A benchmark score is treated as a stable property of the task rather than of the task at collection time.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The mapping from category name to visual appearance is time-indexed, so any fixed test set estimates a frozen snapshot of the task.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate models on obviously time-stamped subsets, such as objects with model years, within existing benchmarks and test for a recency gradient using item metadata; no new collection needed.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Adaptive overfitting to reused test sets is measurable in the foundation-model era: models released later gain more on the canonical test set than on fresh replicas, controlling for capability.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The same test sets have served as development targets for many model generations, and replica studies previously found score drops but debated adaptive overfitting.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] With foundation models whose development loops query public leaderboards and test sets at unprecedented intensity, the canonical-versus-replica gap now grows with release date, indicating accumulated adaptive overfitting rather than pure distribution shift.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Regressing the canonical-minus-replica score gap on model release date across many public checkpoints will show a positive slope robust to capability controls.
why_important: A positive date effect would mean headline benchmark progress partially measures community-level test-set fitting, changing how progress curves should be interpreted.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Earlier replica studies predate the current era; re-running the analysis with the release-date regression framing on the modern model population may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a chronologically spread set of public checkpoints on a canonical set and its existing replica, fit the date-gap regression with accuracy and architecture controls.
main_risk: Later models differ from earlier ones in many correlated ways, and residual confounding could mimic a date effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community largely concluded that adaptive overfitting on major benchmarks is minimal, based on earlier-era evidence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The earlier conclusion was drawn before web-scale pretraining, leaderboard saturation, and automated evaluation harnesses multiplied the channels through which test information reaches model development.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty public checkpoints spanning release years, cached evaluation on canonical plus replica sets, one regression; days of inference at most.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Primary keep of dg21: absorbs C-079 (test-informed selection) as mechanism behind replica-gap growth.

judge_C_meta.anomaly_note: Adaptive overfitting returning in the foundation era would reverse the celebrated replication-era conclusion; release-date-dependent gap is testable.

one_line_idea: General-purpose vision benchmarks embed demographic and geographic confounds that make aggregate scores unrepresentative and cross-model comparisons unstable across subpopulations.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web-collected benchmarks over-represent certain regions, languages, and demographic contexts, and aggregate accuracy is the standard comparison statistic.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model rankings computed on the over-represented strata differ from rankings on under-represented strata often enough that the aggregate leaderboard order is a materially biased estimate of who is best for whom.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stratifying existing benchmarks by inferable geography or context metadata and re-ranking a pool of checkpoints per stratum will show reproducible rank instability, exceeding what bootstrap noise explains.
why_important: Deployment populations rarely match benchmark composition; if rankings are stratum-dependent, a single leaderboard misleads most deployers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Fairness audits of specific tasks exist; a general rank-instability analysis across strata on mainstream benchmarks framed as a leaderboard-validity problem may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Infer or collect stratum metadata for one benchmark, evaluate a model pool per stratum, and test rank stability with paired bootstrap across strata.
main_risk: Inferred stratum labels are error-prone, and errors could either mask or fabricate instability.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The best model on the aggregate benchmark is assumed to be the best choice across deployment contexts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Aggregate scores weight strata by benchmark composition, which is an accident of collection rather than a property of any deployment.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Split one benchmark by an available proxy such as image origin domain and check whether the top-3 model order holds per split; hours with cached predictions.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept in dg19: subgroup/demographic instability has distinct stakes and measurement (strata reranking), though template-identical; flag noted.

one_line_idea: Any fixed-feature-space distance metric for generative image evaluation is structurally gameable, and an adversarial-sensitivity audit should accompany every reported score.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generative image quality is summarized by distances between feature distributions computed in a fixed embedding space, and such scores steer model development.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For any fixed feature extractor there exist generator modifications that improve the score while degrading human-judged quality, and modern training pipelines partially find such directions implicitly, so scores drift from human judgment as optimization pressure increases.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Directly optimizing a generator or a post-hoc filter against the metric will yield samples with better scores and flat-or-worse human preference, and the exploit direction will transfer partially across generators.
why_important: The field's automatic quality numbers are optimization targets; unaudited gameability means reported progress can decouple from perceptual quality without anyone noticing.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Metric gaming is known in principle; a standardized adversarial-sensitivity audit protocol with transferability measurements across current metrics and feature spaces may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Attach a small learnable post-processing module to a fixed generator, optimize it against the metric only, and run a human preference study comparing pre and post samples.
main_risk: Human studies are costly, and small perceptual degradations may need large rater pools to detect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Feature-distance scores are treated as reliable proxies for perceptual quality across the current operating range.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A frozen feature space defines a fixed blind-spot structure, and sustained optimization pressure finds blind spots regardless of which extractor is chosen.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Optimize sample selection, not generation, against the metric from a fixed pool and check whether the score improves while a small human panel sees no improvement; days.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Zero-shot retrieval recall correlates poorly with the end-task utility of embeddings inside retrieval-augmented multimodal pipelines.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Embedding models are ranked by recall-at-k on retrieval benchmarks and then adopted inside retrieval-augmented generation systems whose end metric is answer quality.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Beyond a threshold, recall gains stop translating into end-task gains because errors shift to failure modes recall does not measure, such as retrieving redundant or subtly misleading neighbors, so embedding leaderboards misorder models for pipeline use.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Holding the generator fixed and swapping embedding models across a wide recall range will show a weak, plateauing relation between benchmark recall and end-task answer quality, with rank inversions among the top embedding models.
why_important: Embedding choice is one of the few components teams select purely by leaderboard; a weak proxy link means those selections are close to arbitrary at the top.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Proxy-metric concerns exist in text retrieval; a systematic proxy-validity study for multimodal retrieval-augmented pipelines may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix one multimodal question-answering pipeline, swap eight embedding models of varying benchmark recall, and measure end-task quality with matched retrieval depth.
main_risk: End-task quality depends on generator-retriever interaction effects that one fixed generator may not represent.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher retrieval recall is assumed to yield better retrieval-augmented system performance more or less monotonically.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Recall counts topical hits while the pipeline needs evidence quality, and the two diverge exactly where modern embeddings compete.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three embedding models spanning the leaderboard, one small question set, one fixed generator; compare end-task scores in days.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Multi-task benchmark suite rankings are unstable under reasonable task reweighting, so suite-level leaderboards encode arbitrary editorial weight choices.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Foundation models are compared by averaging scores across task collections whose composition and implicit weighting were set by benchmark authors.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For current model pools, the leaderboard order changes under many defensible reweightings, such as equalizing task families, difficulty, or deployment relevance, so suite rank is an artifact of composition choices rather than a robust capability ordering.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Computing the ranking distribution over a large space of defensible weightings will show that only extreme-gap model pairs have stable order, while adjacent leaderboard positions flip under a substantial fraction of weightings.
why_important: Suite leaderboards are the primary public evidence in model release claims; weight-instability quantifies how much of that evidence is editorial.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Weighting sensitivity is known in social-choice terms; applying a formal ranking-stability analysis with published instability certificates for vision suites may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take per-task public scores for one suite, sample defensible weightings under stated constraints, and publish per-pair order-stability probabilities.
main_risk: Defining the space of defensible weightings is contestable, so results must be shown robust to the definition.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The suite average is treated as a canonical scalar capability measure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging incommensurable task scores requires a weighting choice, and no choice is neutral once models specialize differently.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Per-task scores of five models, one thousand random simplex weightings, count rank flips; an hour on a laptop.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Primary keep of dg19: absorbs C-038 (corruption menus), C-076 (stratified selection), C-100 (usage weighting).

one_line_idea: Repeated-sampling metrics for multimodal generation conflate output diversity with capability, crediting models for stochastic variety rather than reliability.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Best-of-k style metrics reward a model if any of several sampled outputs succeeds, and are increasingly used for multimodal reasoning and generation tasks.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Best-of-k rankings can be driven by sampling temperature and output diversity rather than by the probability of being correct on demand, so they misorder models for single-shot deployment and invert under reliability metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping decoding temperature will move best-of-k scores substantially at fixed model weights, and model rankings under best-of-k will differ from rankings under first-sample accuracy on the same tasks.
why_important: Deployments mostly consume one sample; a leaderboard that rewards lottery-ticket diversity selects models misaligned with use.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The diversity-reliability distinction is discussed for code models; a controlled decomposition for multimodal tasks with temperature-sweep evidence may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several models at multiple temperatures under best-of-k and first-sample metrics on one multimodal task, and quantify how much best-of-k rank is temperature-explainable.
main_risk: Some applications genuinely use best-of-k with verifiers, for which the metric is appropriate, so scope must be stated carefully.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Best-of-k improvements are read as capability improvements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The metric measures the union of k draws, which grows with output entropy independently of per-draw correctness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, three temperatures, best-of-8 versus first-sample on a small task set; an evening.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: distinct falsifiable hypothesis within its cluster after cross-shard comparison; novelty NOT verified (hypothesis-level dedup only, prior-art search pending).

one_line_idea: Micro-averaged accuracy hides that foundation-model progress is concentrated on frequent classes, and macro-averaged evaluation shows much flatter progress curves.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard accuracy weights items equally, which under skewed class distributions weights classes by frequency, and progress claims are made on this micro average.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-scoring historical and current checkpoints with macro-averaged per-class accuracy will show that a disproportionate share of claimed multi-year progress comes from head classes, with tail-class progress substantially slower, changing the shape of the field's progress narrative.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The macro-accuracy progress curve across model generations will be flatter than the micro curve, and the head-tail progress gap will widen for web-pretrained models relative to supervised-era models.
why_important: If progress is frequency-concentrated, capability claims overstate readiness for tail-heavy applications, which are common in specialized domains.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Long-tail evaluation exists as a subfield; applying the macro lens retrospectively to the foundation-model progress narrative across generations may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a chronological pool of public checkpoints with micro and macro metrics on one large benchmark and compare progress-curve slopes.
main_risk: Macro metrics are noisy on rare classes, requiring uncertainty-aware curve comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark progress curves are read as broadly distributed capability growth.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web pretraining data follows heavy-tailed frequency distributions, focusing learning where the metric already concentrates its weight.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Micro and macro scores for five checkpoints spanning several years on one benchmark; hours with cached predictions.

judge_C_adversary.reason: Instance of the same weighting-instability claim (micro-vs-macro arm).

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept: macro-vs-micro progress concentration; see C-008 note.

one_line_idea: Uncontrolled prompt-engineering budgets act as hidden compute in zero-shot comparisons, and equalizing prompt-search effort shrinks or reverses claimed model gaps.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Published zero-shot numbers use prompt sets refined to unknown degrees per model, with the search effort undocumented.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The prompt-search budget is a performance-relevant hidden variable of the same order as model differences, and gaps between models change materially when prompt optimization compute is explicitly equalized.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Running a fixed-budget automated prompt search per model from a common starting set will change reported gaps, in some pairs reversing which model looks better relative to using each model's community-tuned prompts.
why_important: Cross-model zero-shot comparisons underlie adoption claims, and an unequalized tuning budget makes them comparisons of community attention rather than of models.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt sensitivity is well known; formalizing prompt search as accounted compute with budget-equalized comparison protocols may be new for vision-language evaluation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a prompt-search algorithm and budget, apply it identically to several models on two benchmarks, and compare budget-equalized gaps against community-prompt gaps.
main_risk: Search algorithm choice may favor certain models, requiring several search strategies to show robustness.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported zero-shot gaps are treated as intrinsic model differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Popular models accumulate years of community prompt tuning that newer or less popular models never received.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fixed random-search over prompts with an identical trial count for two models on one benchmark; a day.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept from hidden-variable family: prompt-search budget as hidden compute is conceptually distinct from harness variance (it is an optimization-budget confound).

one_line_idea: Linear-probe evaluation encodes a linearity assumption about representation quality, and shallow nonlinear probes rerank vision backbones, undermining probe-based pretraining conclusions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Representation quality of pretrained backbones is standardly compared by accuracy of linear classifiers on frozen features.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Backbones differ in how linearly accessible their information is, not only in how much information they encode, so linear-probe rankings conflate the two and small nonlinear probes will reorder backbones by recovering nonlinearly-encoded information.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing linear probes against capacity-controlled two-layer probes across a pool of backbones will produce reproducible rank changes on some tasks, with disagreement concentrated in backbones trained with objectives that do not encourage linear separability.
why_important: Years of pretraining-method conclusions rest on linear probing; if rankings are probe-dependent, some of those conclusions are protocol artifacts.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Probe-choice sensitivity has been raised in interpretability contexts; a systematic backbone-reranking study framed against the pretraining-evaluation canon may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate ten backbones with linear and matched-budget nonlinear probes on five downstream tasks and quantify rank agreement per task.
main_risk: Nonlinear probes introduce optimization variance, requiring repeated runs to separate signal from probe-training noise.
community_default_belief: [KNOWN FACT] Linear-probe accuracy is the conventional standard for frozen-representation quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Linear accessibility is an objective-dependent property, and objectives differ precisely in this respect across pretraining paradigms.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three backbones, one task, linear versus two-layer probe with equal parameter budget, three seeds; a day.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept but verify prior art: linear-vs-nonlinear probe reranking has adjacent literature.

one_line_idea: Few-shot evaluation variance across support-set draws exceeds the model gaps typically reported, making single-draw few-shot comparisons close to meaningless.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Few-shot results are often reported from one or a few support-set draws, while the draw determines which exemplars define each class.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The across-draw standard deviation of few-shot accuracy for foundation models is comparable to or larger than typical between-model gaps, so many published few-shot orderings would not replicate under redrawn supports.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring the full across-draw distribution for several models will show overlapping distributions for model pairs whose reported point estimates differ by amounts commonly treated as decisive.

one_line_idea: Annotation-vendor ecosystems create test-set leakage paths that deduplication cannot see: the same worker pools and internal guideline documents touch both training-data production and benchmark creation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A small number of annotation vendors and worker platforms service both dataset construction for model training and benchmark annotation, with shared workforces, tooling, and convention documents.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Convention leakage through shared annotation ecosystems aligns training labels with benchmark labels at the level of edge-case handling, giving models trained on vendor-labeled data an unearned benchmark advantage invisible to image-level contamination audits.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Models trained on data labeled under one vendor's conventions will show a measurable edge-case-item advantage on benchmarks annotated under the same conventions, relative to convention-mismatched benchmarks with matched difficulty.
why_important: This is a contamination channel operating on labels rather than images, currently outside every audit framework, and it advantages incumbents with vendor relationships.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Contamination research focuses on data overlap; a convention-leakage framing with an empirical edge-case methodology may be entirely new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify benchmark and training datasets with documented shared versus distinct annotation origins, construct edge-case item sets, and test for convention-aligned accuracy advantages.
main_risk: Annotation provenance is poorly documented, making origin classification the weakest link of the study.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmarks annotated independently of a model's training data are assumed to be uncontaminated tests of it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Labels encode conventions, conventions travel through people and documents, and the industry concentrates both in a few organizations.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare model rankings on edge-case items across two benchmarks of the same task known to use different annotation vendors; days once item sets are built.

one_line_idea: A field-wide bootstrap audit of vision benchmark deltas: a large fraction of published improvements are within test-set resampling noise once paired item-level uncertainty is computed.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision papers overwhelmingly report point-estimate benchmark scores without confidence intervals or paired significance tests, while claimed margins have shrunk over time.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Applying paired item-level bootstrap to a broad sample of published improvement claims will show that a substantial fraction do not exceed resampling noise, and the non-significant fraction has grown over publication years as margins shrank.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Reproducing a systematically sampled set of claimed improvements and computing paired intervals will find a material share of claims whose intervals cover zero, with the share increasing in recent years.
why_important: The field's self-narrative of steady progress depends on trusting small deltas; quantifying their statistical emptiness recalibrates literature-reading and reviewing norms.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Significance critiques exist in adjacent fields; a large-scale executed audit over vision benchmark claims with temporal analysis may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample fifty claimed improvements with reproducible checkpoints, evaluate both models per claim on the original test sets, and compute paired bootstrap intervals per claim.
main_risk: Reproduction failures will contaminate the sample, requiring transparent inclusion criteria and reporting of irreproducible cases as a separate finding.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A published benchmark improvement is presumed to reflect a real difference between methods.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Test sets are finite samples, deltas have shrunk toward the sampling-noise floor, and nothing in the publication pipeline enforces the distinction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pick five recent claimed improvements with public checkpoints, run paired bootstrap on each; days.
