one_line_idea: Leaderboards inflate apparent state-of-the-art through selection: the expected maximum over many noisy submissions exceeds true best performance, and the bias is quantifiable from submission statistics.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Public leaderboards rank by the maximum submitted score, submissions number in the hundreds or thousands, and per-submission scores contain evaluation noise.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The winner's-curse gap between the top reported score and the top submitter's true expected performance is large enough on active leaderboards to account for a visible share of year-over-year state-of-the-art movement.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-evaluating top leaderboard entries on fresh evaluation samples will show systematic regression toward lower scores, with the drop predicted by submission-count and score-variance statistics.
why_important: State-of-the-art numbers anchor claims about the field's frontier; a quantified selection bias changes how leaderboard records should be read and designed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Winner's-curse effects are understood in statistics and machine learning competitions; an empirical quantification on major vision leaderboards with a correction protocol may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one leaderboard with accessible top entries, re-evaluate leaders on a held-out replica sample and compare observed regression with selection-bias theory predictions.
main_risk: Fresh evaluation samples differ from the original distribution, confounding selection regression with distribution shift, which the analysis must separate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The leaderboard top score is treated as the field's true current capability level.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Maximizing over noisy estimates is a biased estimator of the maximum, and the bias grows with the number of attempts, which leaderboards maximize by design.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Simulate the leaderboard's submission process with realistic noise to size the expected bias, then spot-check one top entry on a replica set; days.

one_line_idea: The vision benchmark ecosystem has low effective dimensionality: most benchmarks rank models nearly identically, so new benchmarks add publication events but little measurement information.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dozens of benchmarks are used to compare vision foundation models, each presented as measuring a distinct capability.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The cross-model score matrix over current benchmarks is dominated by one or two principal components, implying most benchmarks are re-measurements of a general factor plus noise, and claimed capability distinctions are mostly unsupported.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Factor analysis of a large model-by-benchmark score matrix will show a dominant first factor explaining most variance, with few benchmarks carrying reliable unique variance after accounting for it.
why_important: Benchmark proliferation consumes community effort and shapes narratives about distinct capabilities; knowing the true dimensionality redirects benchmark design toward genuinely orthogonal measurements.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Correlation among benchmarks is informally acknowledged; a formal psychometric treatment of the vision benchmark ecosystem with reliability-corrected unique-variance estimates may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble a score matrix for many public models across many benchmarks, run factor analysis with split-half reliability correction, and report per-benchmark unique information.
main_risk: Model selection into the matrix is not random, and family clustering could inflate the apparent general factor.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Each established benchmark is assumed to measure a meaningfully distinct capability dimension.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Benchmarks are built from similar web imagery with similar protocols by a community with shared assumptions, so their measurements plausibly collapse onto a common axis.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Score matrix from public leaderboard data for thirty models by fifteen benchmarks, one factor analysis; hours, no inference.

one_line_idea: The same checkpoint scores materially differently across popular evaluation harnesses, and harness variance is an unbudgeted error term in every cross-paper comparison.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multiple open-source harnesses implement the same benchmarks with differing preprocessing, prompt formatting, answer extraction, and scoring code, and papers cite scores without specifying harness details.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-harness score variance for identical checkpoints on identical benchmarks is comparable to typical between-model gaps, especially for vision-language tasks where extraction and formatting differ most.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Running fixed checkpoints through several harnesses will produce per-model score ranges that overlap adjacent models' ranges, making harness-unspecified comparisons ambiguous between real and tooling differences.
why_important: The field's comparison fabric assumes score portability across tooling; measuring harness variance either validates or breaks that assumption with immediate reporting-standard implications.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Harness discrepancies are reported anecdotally in issue trackers; a systematic cross-harness variance quantification for vision and multimodal benchmarks may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate five checkpoints on three benchmarks through three harnesses each, decompose variance into model, harness, and interaction components.
main_risk: Harness differences sometimes reflect legitimate protocol disagreements rather than bugs, requiring careful taxonomy of the discrepancy sources.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A benchmark score is assumed to be a harness-independent property of the model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The benchmark is a specification, the harness is an implementation, and unversioned implementations of underspecified protocols diverge as a rule.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One multimodal checkpoint, one benchmark, two harnesses with default settings; two numbers in hours.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Primary keep of dg16 harness-variance umbrella: absorbs C-031, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-053, C-098; one crossed-design audit, not six papers.

one_line_idea: Silent test-informed model selection is endemic: development practices leak test-set signal into checkpoint choice, and a leakage-audit protocol can measure the resulting inflation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Papers select the reported checkpoint among training runs and variants, and the selection criterion often includes or correlates with the official test score through repeated evaluation during development.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Test-informed selection inflates reported scores by an amount estimable from the number of implicit test queries during development, and this inflation accounts for part of the gap between published numbers and independent reproductions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Simulating realistic development loops with varying test-consultation frequency will produce inflation curves, and independently retrained reproductions of published pipelines will land below published numbers by amounts consistent with those curves.
why_important: The practice is universal, unmeasured, and invisible in papers; quantifying it explains reproduction gaps and motivates held-back evaluation infrastructure.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Adaptive data analysis theory covers this abstractly; an empirical inflation measurement calibrated to actual vision development practices may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run controlled development loops on a private split with scripted selection policies of varying test exposure, measuring inflation against a truly held-out split.
main_risk: Real development practices are heterogeneous and self-reported badly, making the simulation's realism contestable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported test scores are treated as unbiased despite the checkpoint having been selected with test feedback.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every glance at the test score during development is a query that spends statistical validity, and nobody counts the queries.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One task, one architecture, two selection policies differing only in test-consultation, ten runs each; compare held-out gaps within days.

judge_A_dedup.reason: Test-informed selection is the causal mechanism behind C-032's adaptive-overfitting measurement; one program. Merge.

judge_B_feasibility_meta.note: KEEP in disagreement with Judge A: the controlled dev-loop is the causal version of C-032's observational regression and is cheap; keep both, they triangulate.

one_line_idea: Published ablation tables systematically overstate component importance because ablations are run once, at one scale, on one seed: a variance-aware re-ablation study.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Method papers justify design choices with ablation tables that typically report single-run deltas for each removed component.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-running representative published ablations with multiple seeds and at multiple scales will show that a large fraction of component deltas are within seed noise or reverse sign across scales, meaning published ablations substantially overstate how much each component matters.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A multi-seed multi-scale re-ablation of components from several published vision methods will find a material share of components whose contribution is statistically indistinguishable from zero or scale-inconsistent.
why_important: Ablations are the field's causal evidence about what works; if they are noise-level measurements, method-design lore built on them is unreliable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Seed-variance concerns are known; a dedicated re-ablation audit of published component claims in vision may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select three reproducible methods, re-run their ablation tables with five seeds at two scales, and compare published deltas with estimated intervals.
main_risk: Faithful reproduction of published training setups is hard, and discrepancies could be blamed on reproduction rather than variance.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Ablation tables are read as reliable evidence of each component's contribution.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A single-run delta is a sample of size one from a noisy distribution, reported without any uncertainty and selected for publication when it looks clean.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One published ablation row, five seeds, check whether the interval covers zero; days of moderate compute.

judge_C_adversary.reason: Single-seed ablation deltas are the ablation-level case of the seed lottery.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Kept in dg18: ablation-table variance targets a different object (component claims) than leaderboard deltas.

one_line_idea: Effective-robustness analysis via linear fits on accuracy scatter plots breaks down near the accuracy ceiling, and conclusions about which interventions confer robustness flip under ceiling-aware models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Robustness beyond baseline is commonly quantified as vertical displacement from a linear in-distribution versus out-of-distribution accuracy trend fitted across models.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The linear-trend methodology produces systematic artifacts as models approach accuracy ceilings, misattributing compression effects to robustness, and re-analysis with nonlinear or logit-transformed fits overturns some published effective-robustness conclusions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Refitting published effective-robustness analyses with ceiling-aware functional forms will change which model classes appear to have above-trend robustness, particularly among the highest-accuracy models.
why_important: Effective robustness drives claims about which training paradigms confer genuine distributional robustness, influencing pretraining strategy choices.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Logit-transform practices exist in parts of the literature; a systematic demonstration that methodology choice reverses headline robustness conclusions may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reassemble public accuracy pairs across many models, fit linear and ceiling-aware forms, and compare which models show above-trend robustness under each.
main_risk: Functional-form choice is itself contestable, so conclusions must be presented as sensitivity ranges rather than a new single truth.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Vertical displacement from the linear trend is treated as a valid measure of intrinsic robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Accuracy pairs live in a bounded space where linear trends cannot hold globally, and the interesting models cluster exactly where the boundedness bites.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Refit one published scatter with a logit-transformed model and compare above-trend classifications; hours with public data.

one_line_idea: Distribution-shift benchmarks conflate multiple shift types into single scores, and factorizing shifts reveals that models robust on the benchmark are robust to only some factors deployments care about.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Popular shift benchmarks mix style changes, viewpoint changes, object-context changes, and capture-pipeline changes in unquantified proportions behind one aggregate score.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model robustness is factor-specific, and aggregate shift scores hide large factor-level differences between models, so two models with equal benchmark robustness can behave oppositely on any given deployment's dominant shift factor.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Decomposing existing shift benchmarks into factor-labeled strata and re-scoring model pools will show low cross-factor correlation of robustness within models and factor-level rank reversals between models.
why_important: Deployment shift is factor-specific, so a factor-blind robustness score cannot inform any actual deployment decision despite being used for exactly that.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Shift taxonomies exist conceptually; delivering factor labels for existing benchmarks plus a factor-level robustness atlas of public models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate shift factors for one popular benchmark's items, compute factor-stratified robustness for many checkpoints, and measure cross-factor robustness correlation.
main_risk: Factor annotation is subjective for compound shifts, requiring multi-annotator protocols and factor-purity checks.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A model that scores well on a shift benchmark is considered generally distribution-robust.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Robustness mechanisms such as augmentation, data diversity, and architecture each target specific invariances, so uniform robustness across factors has no reason to exist.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Label two contrasting factors on a benchmark subset, check whether model rankings agree across the two strata; days including annotation.

one_line_idea: Fixed-epsilon adversarial evaluation is incomparable across models with different preprocessing and native resolutions, making cross-model robustness tables silently inconsistent.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Adversarial robustness is reported at fixed pixel-space perturbation budgets, while models consume inputs through different normalizations, resolutions, and value ranges.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A fixed nominal budget corresponds to different effective perturbation strengths across preprocessing pipelines, so cross-model robustness comparisons at equal epsilon are comparing unequal attacks, and perceptually-calibrated budgets change the rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-evaluating a pool of models under perceptually-equalized rather than nominally-equalized budgets will change robustness rankings, with the largest movements for models whose preprocessing differs most from the convention.
why_important: Robustness tables guide defense research and safety claims; unequal effective budgets mean the tables embed a hidden preprocessing subsidy.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Input-space versus perceptual-space budget debates exist; a quantified demonstration of ranking distortion across modern heterogeneous pipelines may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a perceptual perturbation budget via human-calibrated or psychophysically motivated metrics, re-run standard attacks on a model pool under both budget definitions, and compare rankings.
main_risk: Perceptual budget definitions are contestable, so several alternatives must agree for the conclusion to stand.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Equal nominal epsilon is assumed to define a fair comparison across models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The attack budget lives in the input space of each model, and those spaces are not the same space when preprocessing differs.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two models with different native resolutions, one attack at fixed nominal budget, measure effective perceptual distance of successful perturbations; a day.

one_line_idea: Corruption-robustness gains from augmentation research are substantially overfitting to the benchmark's corruption menu, and generalization to held-out corruption families is much weaker than reported averages suggest.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Robustness methods are developed and compared against a fixed public menu of corruption types, and the same menu is used for years of method iterations.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The community has been implicitly fitting the corruption menu, so method rankings on the standard menu poorly predict rankings on freshly designed held-out corruption families, and the field's measured robustness progress partially evaporates under menu replacement.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating historical robustness methods on a new disjoint corruption menu will show compressed method gaps and ranking changes relative to the standard menu, with later methods losing more of their advantage than earlier ones.
why_important: If robustness progress is menu-specific, deployed systems inherit less protection than the literature promises, and benchmark rotation becomes necessary.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Held-out corruption concerns motivated some benchmark variants; a longitudinal overfitting analysis across method generations with menu replacement may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Design a validated held-out corruption menu, evaluate a chronological sequence of published robustness methods on both menus, and test for a method-age interaction in the transfer gap.
main_risk: New corruptions must be validated as realistic and difficulty-matched, or transfer gaps could reflect difficulty rather than overfitting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Gains on the standard corruption suite are read as general corruption robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Years of method selection against a fixed target is a textbook recipe for target-specific adaptation, whatever the target.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three methods spanning years, five newly implemented corruptions, compare standard-menu versus new-menu gaps; days.

one_line_idea: Vision models certified robust by standard suites fail on temporal shift: robustness leaderboard leaders lose their advantage on data collected years after their training cutoffs.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Robustness evaluation emphasizes synthetic corruptions and curated shift sets, while the mundane shift every deployment faces is the world changing over time.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Ranking models by standard robustness suites poorly predicts ranking by accuracy retention on temporally newer data, because temporal drift stresses semantic and distributional changes the suites do not represent.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Correlating suite-based robustness scores with temporal retention measured on collection-date-stamped data will yield weak correlation across a model pool, with some suite leaders showing below-average temporal retention.
why_important: Temporal drift is the universal deployment shift; if the field's robustness measurements do not predict it, robustness research is optimizing a proxy detached from its purpose.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal evaluation exists in niche studies; positioning temporal retention as a validity test for the robustness-benchmark ecosystem may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble date-stamped evaluation sets spanning several years for stable categories, evaluate a model pool, and correlate temporal retention with standard robustness scores.
main_risk: Date-stamped data collection must control for concurrent changes in image sources and camera technology that are not the drift of interest.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Models topping robustness leaderboards are expected to age gracefully in deployment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The suites test invariance to pixel-level and style perturbations while time changes the objects, contexts, and category statistics themselves.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two models with equal suite robustness, evaluated on date-partitioned items of one dataset with timestamps; hours if metadata exists.

one_line_idea: Spurious-correlation benchmarks contain their own meta-spurious cues: models can score well on debiasing tests by exploiting artifacts of how the tests were constructed.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmarks testing reliance on spurious features are constructed by deliberately decorrelating or counter-correlating attributes, a process that leaves statistical fingerprints in the resulting data.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The construction process of debiasing benchmarks introduces secondary regularities, such as selection-induced attribute distributions or editing artifacts, that models can exploit to pass without acquiring the intended invariance, so benchmark passage does not certify debiasing.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Probing classifiers will detect construction fingerprints in debiasing benchmarks at above-chance rates, and models fine-tuned to pass the benchmark will fail alternative debiasing tests constructed with different methodologies.
why_important: Debiasing benchmarks gatekeep fairness and robustness claims; if passable via meta-artifacts, the certification they provide is hollow.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Artifact critiques target ordinary benchmarks; turning the artifact lens onto the debiasing benchmarks themselves may be a new recursion.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train fingerprint probes on construction metadata for two debiasing benchmarks, then test whether benchmark-passing models transfer to methodologically independent debiasing tests.
main_risk: Distinguishing exploitation of fingerprints from genuine invariance requires careful causal test design.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Passing a spurious-correlation benchmark is taken as evidence a model does not rely on the spurious feature.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Any dataset constructed to violate natural correlations is itself unnatural in detectable ways, and models optimize against whatever regularities exist.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train a shallow probe to classify benchmark membership of images against natural counterparts; above-chance accuracy in hours signals fingerprints.

one_line_idea: Certified-robustness guarantees do not predict empirical security under realistic attacks: certification radius and practical attack success are weakly related across defended models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Certified defenses report provable robustness radii under specific norms and smoothing assumptions, and these certificates are presented as security evidence.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because certificates cover threat models that real attackers ignore, the correlation between certified radius and empirical attack success under realistic unrestricted attacks is weak across defended models, making certificates a poor ranking signal for practical security.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Ranking certified models by radius and separately by empirical robustness against a strong realistic attack battery will show low rank correlation, with some highly-certified models among the empirically weakest.
why_important: Certificates carry the rhetorical weight of proofs, and consumers may choose defenses by certified numbers that do not track the threats they face.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The gap between certified and empirical robustness is acknowledged conceptually; a systematic rank-correlation study across the certified-defense model zoo may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect public certified checkpoints, evaluate certified radii and empirical robustness under a standardized realistic attack battery, and compute rank correlations.
main_risk: Realistic attack batteries are contestable, so the battery must include diverse attack philosophies to be credible.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Larger certified radii are assumed to indicate more practically secure models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A proof about one norm-ball says nothing about the attack surface outside it, which is where practical attacks operate.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three certified checkpoints, one realistic attack, compare empirical ordering with certified ordering; a day.

one_line_idea: Object-hallucination benchmarks for captioning models measure language co-occurrence priors more than visual grounding, and a blind-model control quantifies exactly how much.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Hallucination benchmarks score whether described objects are present, using item sets built from natural images whose object co-occurrence statistics mirror web text priors.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large share of hallucination-benchmark variance is predictable from language priors alone, so models are being ranked substantially on prior management rather than perception, and prior-decorrelated item sets change the rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A text-only predictor given object context but no image will predict hallucination-benchmark outcomes well above chance, and re-ranking models on prior-decorrelated items will differ from standard rankings.
why_important: Hallucination scores drive safety narratives about multimodal models; measuring the language-prior share converts an ambiguous metric into an interpretable one.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Language-prior critiques exist for question answering; a quantified prior-share decomposition for modern hallucination benchmarks may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a language-prior model to predict benchmark outcomes without images, then build a decorrelated item subset and re-rank multimodal models on it.
main_risk: Decorrelated items may be unnatural scenes, trading one validity problem for another, so naturalness must be human-audited.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Hallucination benchmark scores are read as measuring visual grounding fidelity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The benchmark's positive and negative cases were sampled from a world whose statistics the language model already knows.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run a text-only model on the benchmark's judgment tasks with images withheld; above-chance performance in an evening quantifies the leak.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Primary keep of dg23: absorbs C-091 (salience priors) and C-096 (count priors); one prior-decorrelated-items program.

one_line_idea: Visual-grounding scores of multimodal models collapse under image-swap consistency tests: models answer identically when the image is replaced, exposing text-shortcut reliance the benchmarks never check.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Grounding benchmarks score answer correctness given the paired image, and do not routinely test whether the answer changes when the image is swapped or removed.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A significant fraction of correct answers on grounding benchmarks survive image substitution, meaning measured grounding is substantially text-driven, and consistency-adjusted scores that require answer sensitivity to the image will rerank current models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring answer invariance under controlled image swaps will reveal high invariance rates on several benchmarks, and consistency-adjusted scoring will produce different model orderings than raw accuracy.
why_important: Grounding is the core claimed capability of multimodal models; scores that cannot distinguish looking from guessing certify the wrong thing.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Image-ablation controls appear in isolated papers; consistency-adjusted scoring as a standard reporting layer with a cross-benchmark audit may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several benchmarks and models, re-run evaluation with distractor image swaps and compute answer-invariance rates plus consistency-adjusted rankings.
main_risk: Swap images must be plausibility-matched, or invariance could reflect the swap's detectability rather than text shortcuts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A correct answer given the image is counted as evidence the model used the image.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Correctness is a joint product of priors and perception, and the benchmarks never separate the factors.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one benchmark subset, answers with original versus randomly swapped images; invariance rate by the end of the day.

one_line_idea: Reported multimodal reasoning gains on text-rich benchmarks are mostly optical-character-recognition gains in disguise, separable by transcribed-input ablations.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmarks involving documents, charts, and text-in-image are scored end-to-end, so recognition quality and reasoning quality contribute inseparably to the reported number.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-model differences on text-rich visual benchmarks are dominated by recognition quality, and providing ground-truth transcriptions equalizes models far more than reasoning-difference narratives predict.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating models with and without oracle transcriptions will show large gap compression under oracle input, attributing most of the original gaps to recognition rather than reasoning.
why_important: Model cards and marketing attribute text-rich benchmark leads to reasoning; misattribution distorts both buyer decisions and research investment.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Component ablations exist in document-understanding research; a systematic recognition-versus-reasoning decomposition across current multimodal models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select text-rich benchmarks with recoverable transcriptions, evaluate a model pool with raw images versus oracle-text-plus-image input, and decompose the gaps.
main_risk: Oracle transcription changes the task interface and could disadvantage models tuned for pixel-space text reading.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Leads on text-rich visual benchmarks are read as multimodal reasoning superiority.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The bottleneck component determines the score, and recognition is plausibly the bottleneck for most current systems.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, two models with a known gap, oracle-transcription ablation; a day.

one_line_idea: Video-understanding benchmarks remain largely solvable from one or a few frames even for the newest foundation models, so temporal-understanding claims are still uncertified.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Single-frame solvability was demonstrated for older video benchmarks, and new benchmarks plus new models have since appeared with renewed temporal-understanding claims.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The single-frame shortcut persists in the current benchmark generation because item construction economics did not change, so current temporal-capability claims rest on benchmarks that still do not require time.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Frame-ablated and frame-shuffled evaluations of current models on current video benchmarks will recover most of the full-video scores, with genuinely temporal items forming a small identifiable minority.
why_important: Video capability drives major compute investments and product claims; certifying it with time-indifferent benchmarks misleads the entire stack.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The critique is established for older benchmarks; the contrarian contribution is demonstrating its persistence in the newest benchmark generation and providing a certified temporal-item subset, which may be undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run single-frame, sparse-frame, and shuffled-frame ablations for several current models on the newest video benchmarks, and publish per-benchmark temporal-necessity scores.
main_risk: Some models degrade under frame ablation for interface rather than capability reasons, requiring input-format controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] New video benchmarks are assumed to have fixed the single-frame solvability problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The incentive to produce many items cheaply still favors questions answerable from appearances rather than dynamics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One new benchmark, one model, middle-frame-only evaluation; recovery fraction by tomorrow.

judge_A_meta.judge_notes: Primary keep of dg24: absorbs C-094 (multi-image); single-input-sufficiency audit across benchmark families.

one_line_idea: Safety evaluations of multimodal models measure refusal-style pattern matching rather than harm-relevant capability, and style-normalized re-evaluation reorders safety leaderboards.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multimodal safety benchmarks score whether models refuse or comply on curated prompt sets, with grading often keyed to refusal phrasing.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Safety scores are dominated by superficial refusal-style alignment with graders, so models can score safely while remaining capable of harm under rephrased elicitation, and style-normalized adversarial evaluation will substantially reorder safety rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Applying systematic elicitation variations and grading on outcome rather than style will show large per-model score movements and ranking changes relative to standard safety benchmark results.
why_important: Safety leaderboards inform deployment gates and public trust; if they measure etiquette rather than safety, the gates are decorative.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Jailbreak research shows brittleness; converting that insight into a validity critique with style-normalized safety scoring for multimodal models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate models on one safety benchmark under elicitation-varied prompts with outcome-based human grading, and compare rankings with the standard protocol.
main_risk: Outcome-based grading of unsafe content requires careful ethics protocols and restricted handling.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher refusal-benchmark scores are taken to mean safer models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Refusal is a surface behavior trained separately from capability, and graders keyed to surface forms measure the training of the surface.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty benchmark items, five elicitation variants each, one model, outcome-graded; days under proper safety protocols.

one_line_idea: The assumption that higher pretraining data quality uniformly improves downstream performance is wrong: quality filtering helps some downstream tasks while measurably hurting others, and the trade-off is hidden by suite averages.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Data-quality filtering is applied globally during pretraining under the assumption that cleaner data is better for downstream performance in general.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Quality filters remove data strata, such as low-quality imagery, unusual viewpoints, and degraded captures, that specific downstream tasks depend on, so per-task analysis will reveal reproducible harms from filtering that aggregate reporting conceals.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Pretraining matched models on filtered versus unfiltered pools and evaluating on a broad task battery will show a subset of tasks, plausibly those involving degraded or atypical imagery, where the unfiltered model wins consistently.
why_important: Filtering decisions are made once and inherited by every downstream user; unmeasured per-task harms mean some application communities are silently paying for others' gains.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-quality research reports aggregate gains; a harm-focused per-task decomposition of filtering effects may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain paired mid-scale models on filtered and unfiltered versions of one pool, evaluate on a task battery including degraded-input tasks, and test for reproducible per-task reversals.
main_risk: Mid-scale results may not extrapolate, and the harmed-task set could differ at production scale.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Data-quality filtering is assumed beneficial or neutral for essentially all downstream uses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Quality is defined relative to a curator's aesthetic, and tasks that live in the discarded stratum lose their training signal by definition.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate existing public checkpoints known to differ mainly in filtering strictness on two degraded-input tasks; a day if such checkpoint pairs exist.

one_line_idea: English-centric class names and prompts are an ignored evaluation assumption: multilingual re-evaluation of zero-shot vision models changes rankings and reveals language-dependent capability profiles.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Zero-shot vision evaluation almost universally uses English class names and prompts, while models differ in multilingual pretraining exposure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model rankings under non-English class vocabularies differ substantially from English rankings, and English evaluation systematically overstates the relative quality of English-dominant models for the majority-world deployment contexts where other languages define the labels.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating a model pool with translated and localized class vocabularies across several languages will show reproducible ranking changes and per-model language sensitivity profiles diverging from the English-based leaderboard.
why_important: Global deployments interface with local vocabularies; an English-only evaluation convention misestimates model value for most of the world's users.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multilingual vision-language work exists; framing English evaluation as a ranking-distorting assumption with a cross-language rank-stability audit may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build validated class-name translations for one benchmark in five languages, evaluate a model pool per language, and quantify ranking stability across languages.
main_risk: Translation quality and cultural category mismatches must be controlled, or effects could reflect bad translations rather than model properties.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] English-based zero-shot scores are treated as language-neutral measures of visual capability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The text encoder is half the zero-shot system, and its quality is sharply language-dependent in ways the convention never measures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, two languages, three models; rank-stability check in a day with existing translation resources.
